# PREFACE

*...bringing them to light: so that men, eager for this most excellent and most useful **art**<note>original: "ars." In this period, "art" referred to a practical skill or craft based on specific rules, as opposed to pure theory.</note>, may be able to use and enjoy them. But someone will say that I, through these editions of mine, bring more harm than benefit to the **commonwealth**<note>original: "reipub." (reipublicae). In the 16th century, this often referred to the "Republic of Letters"—the international community of scholars—as much as the general public.</note>, since the art is vain and is no **science**<note>original: "scientia." Here meaning a systematic body of knowledge based on certain, demonstrable principles.</note> at all: because it deals not with things that are entirely certain, but with things that are uncertain and rarely happen—indeed, most rarely, or perhaps never—according to the opinions of many. For they claim that no one, in our own or the preceding century, has actually performed those things which the **writers** of this art so magnificently and in so many ways promise. Since it therefore lacks its intended **goal**<note>original: "fine." In the Aristotelian sense, the "finis" or "end" is the purpose for which a thing exists or the result it is meant to achieve.</note>, and since all things are done for the sake of a goal, it follows that there is neither art nor science here, and that those who engage in these things are ridiculous and foolish, or else believe in shiftless impostors. To these critics, enough and more has already been responded by excellent and most learned **philosophers** through certain demonstrations, and the **truth** of this art has been proven (especially...*

# PROPOSITIONS OR
## THE GREATEST MAXIMS OF THE
### *Chemical Art.* <note>original: "Ars Chemica." While "Chemica" eventually became modern chemistry, here it refers to the "Art" of alchemy.</note>

---

### PROPOSITION I.

Every pure and clean extract taken from its ore <term>minera: the raw mineral or ore from which metals are extracted</term>, from stones, or from foreign matter, which—without some preparation—does not melt like wax, is unsuitable for this work. From this, it is concluded that all metals are excluded, as are all species of Marcasite <term>Marchasitæ: a term used then for various mineral sulfides that look like metallic ores but are brittle</term>, glass, crystal, coral, and all pearls which do not liquefy in fire.

### *Proposition II.*

Every sublimable substance <term>sublimabile: a substance capable of "sublimation," turning directly from a solid into a vapor when heated</term> which adheres to the sides of the vessel, preventing the sight of foreign matter within the vessel, is remote from and unsuitable for this undertaking <note>original: "negocio," referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy</note>. For this reason, all four principal spirits <term>spiritus principales: in alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances that vaporize easily</term> are especially excluded: namely, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and every kind of tutty <term>tutiæ: zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term> and magnesia <term>magnesiæ: a term used historically for various minerals, often manganese or magnetic iron ore</term>.

<summary>This page introduces the foundational rules of the alchemical "Chemical Art," defining which substances are unsuitable for the work. It specifically excludes non-melting minerals, metals, and volatile "spirits" like mercury and sulfur from this particular process.</summary>

<keywords>Propositions, Alchemy, Marcasite, Sublimation, Four Spirits, Mercury, Arsenic, Sulfur, Tutty, Magnesia</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Propositions or Maxims of the Chemical Art" from the previous page. While the previous section excluded common metals and volatile "spirits" like mercury and sulfur, this page further defines the boundaries of the alchemical materials by excluding animal and vegetable matter.</meta>

### PROPOSITION III.

Every mineral that does not possess the nature of earth is foreign and hostile to this work. From this, all things that come from animals are excluded, such as hair, blood, flesh, dung, eggs, and the like; and also all animals themselves, such as turtles, beetles <note>original: "caragdi," likely referring to beetles or other hard-shelled organisms often mentioned in catalogs of natural history</note>, moles, frogs, bees, and similar creatures.

### PROPOSITION IV.

Any thing that is animate, or that proceeds from inanimate things <note>The text here says "inanimatis" (inanimate), though the examples provided—wine and vegetables—are organic. The author is likely distinguishing between the "living" mineral used in alchemy and ordinary organic or inert matter.</note>, is unsuitable for this greater art. From this proposition, all animal superfluities <term>superfluitates: bodily secretions or waste products</term> are especially excluded, as well as all vegetables and everything that comes from them—such as wine, "burning water" <term>aqua ardens: distilled alcohol or spirits</term>, oil, honey, urine, semen, and similar things.

### PROPOSITION V.

Anything which cannot be blackened, whitened, and reddened <note>These three colors represent the core stages of the alchemical process: Nigredo (black), Albedo (white), and Rubedo (red)</note> by fire within one hour of a natural day, does not enter into the composition of this work as the principle of masculinity <note>original: "masculineitatis," referring to the active or "male" agent in the alchemical "marriage" or reaction</note>.

<meta>catchword: Propo-</meta>

<summary>These propositions define the "Chemical Art" by excluding all animal and vegetable substances, as well as any mineral that cannot undergo the three essential color changes (black, white, and red) under the influence of fire.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, animal substances, vegetable substances, aqua ardens, masculine principle, Nigredo, Albedo, Rubedo, alchemical maxims</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Propositions or Maxims of the Chemical Art." Having previously excluded organic matter and defined the "masculine" principle, the text now defines the "feminine" principle and the necessity of duality and simplicity in the alchemical process.</meta>

### *Proposition VI.*

Everything that lacks red smoke <note>original: "fumo rubeo"; in alchemical practice, the appearance of colored vapors often signaled the presence of specific spirits or the success of a sublimation</note>, when enclosed in a small vessel over a proper fire, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the feminine principle <note>original: "foemineitatis"; the passive or receptive partner in the "chemical marriage"</note>. From the two aforementioned maxims, alums and salts are excluded, as well as every kind of borax <term>baurachiorum: alkaline salts or boraxes used as fluxes</term> and vitriols <term>gignarum: likely referring to metallic salts or vitriolic "seeds"</term>, and all liquids derived from them.

### *Proposition VII.*

No single thing <note>original: "vnius numeri," literally "of one number"</note> can complete a work of a higher order. From this it is especially gathered that the philosophers' stone is made from two things—namely, the male and the female, or the red and the white <note>In alchemy, "red and white" often refer to the two primary stages or reagents: the white stone (which transmutates to silver) and the red stone (which transmutates to gold)</note>.

### *Proposition VIII.*

Whatever cannot be completed in one vessel and in a single sequence <note>original: "vno numero"</note> is unsuitable for this work. And by this rule, the use of multiple vessels is especially excluded <note>Alchemy often emphasized "One Vessel, One Furnace, One Way" to signify the purity and unity of the Great Work</note>.

### *Proposition IX.*

Whatever, within the space of one hundred days

to more is not able to finish such perfection, and the making of gold and silver <note>original: "aurum & argentum"; the text suggests that simply trying to manufacture bullion for profit is contrary to the true, "perfect" alchemical art</note> is hostile to this work. ### *Proposition X.*

### Proposition XI.

Every medicine <term>medicine: in alchemy, this refers to the refined substance or Elixir that heals "diseased" base metals into pure gold</term> that cannot multiply itself infinitely is not part of the intention of the work of the higher order <note>original: "operis maioris ordinis"; this refers to the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the highest level of alchemical achievement</note>. From this, it is chiefly gathered that the multiplication of this work is one part of the aforementioned medicine. For the redness <note>original: "rubedinem"; the Rubedo or final "Red Stage" of the alchemical process</note>, the aforementioned vessel should be placed with twelve parts with a fire of three lights <note>original: "igne trium luminum"; likely referring to three wicks or oil lamps, signifying a specific, increased level of heat</note> for fifteen days, and it will arrive at the ultimate redness, and it will be the Elixir for perfect red <term>red: the alchemical code for Gold</term>, and in this way, you can multiply it infinitely.

### Proposition XII.

Whatever exceeds the value of one ounce of pure gold is not of the intention of the higher order. And from this it is chiefly gathered that those things which compose the physical stone <term>physical stone: another name for the Philosopher's Stone</term>, if they exceed one ounce of pure gold in cost, they are not of the intention of the higher order. And from this it chiefly follows that 15 grains of ferment <term>ferment: the "yeast" or starter substance added to the alchemical matter to trigger transformation</term> are suitable for the work of the higher order, because they are purchased at a cheap price <note>original: "vili precio"; a common alchemical trope is that the "First Matter" of the Stone is something common and inexpensive, overlooked by the ignorant</note>.

### and last.

Only that which is composed of **incombustible oil** <term>incombustible oil: in alchemy, this refers to a "fixed" or permanent substance that can withstand the heat of fire without burning away, often symbolizing the "soul" of the matter</term>, and of **fusible salt** <term>fusible salt: a salt that can be melted or liquefied; this represents the "body" or the crystallized structure of the Stone</term>, is friendly to this art. From this it is chiefly gathered that the **physical stone** <note>original: "lapis Physicus"; the Philosopher's Stone</note> is composed of incombustible oil and fusible salt.

### PHILOSOPHY

a 2

...thins the air. <note>The word fragment "-ti" from the previous page completes "extenuati," referring to the thinning or refining of the air.</note> Know, O **Assembly**, that the density <term>density: original "spissitudo," referring to the physical thickness, weight, or "grossness" of matter</term> of the four beginnings <note>original: "quatuor initiorum," the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth</note> rests in the earth alone. This is because the dense part of fire falls into the air; the dense part of air, along with that which is gathered from the dense part of fire, falls into the water. The dense part of water, and that which is joined together from the dense part of fire and air, rests in the earth. Thus the density of these four rests in the earth, and they are joined together within it. Therefore, the earth itself is denser than all the other elements, as is clearly apparent and can be seen. Fire, however, is rarer <term>rarer: original "rarior," meaning more subtle, thin, or less physically substantial</term> than the others; and just as the earth, being denser, is lower, so fire is higher and more noble. Air is indeed less rare than fire, and water in turn is less rare than air. For everything cold and moist is of less rarity than that which is hot and moist. And earth is of less rarity than water, because it is cold and dry; and everything cold and dry is less rare than that which is cold and moist.

Therefore, before all things, God created the four elements, and afterward, He created whatever He willed from them—namely, various natures, some of which He created from only one element.

For they rot and are born because nature—which governs the substance, destroys it, and converts it into powder and nothingness—then renews, repeats, and gives birth to it frequently. For the very thing that kills is that which also gives life. Therefore, direct your [attention]...

# THE ASSEMBLY

**Ardarius** said: I will describe to you the **management of the stone** <note>original: "Regimen lapidis"; the specific set of rules, temperatures, and stages required to successfully create the Philosopher's Stone</note> and its composition. Take the hidden and honorable secret, which is **white magnesia** <note>original: "magnefies alba"; in alchemy, this is not modern magnesium but a cryptic name for a primary material, often associated with the "white" stage of purification</note>, which is mixed with the **living spirit** <note>original: "vivo"; likely referring to *argentum vivum* or quicksilver/mercury</note>. But you must not take it unless it is pure and clean; place it in its own vessel, and pray to God that He might grant you to see this greatest stone. 

Then cook it slowly. When you have drawn it out, see if it has become black; and if it is so, you have managed it excellently. But if it is not, manage it with the **white secret**, which is the greatest mystery, until the **blackness** <term>nigredo</term> <note>The first major stage of the alchemical "Great Work," symbolizing the death or decomposition of the old form before rebirth</note> appears—and indeed, a pure blackness, which lasts for exactly forty days. 

Afterward, grind it with its preparations, which are the **flower of copper** <note>original: "flos aeris"; typically refers to the green film or "verdigris" that forms on copper, used as a reagent</note> and **Indian gold** <note>original: "aurum Indicum"; a poetic or technical term for a specific yellow-colored precipitate or refined substance</note>, whose root is made of **saffron ointment** <note>original: "unguento croceo"</note> and **fixed alum**. Therefore, cook this diligently for forty days; when this is completed, God will show you the beginning of the stone. 

Cook it again, and soak it with the remaining **gum** <note>original: "gumi"; alchemical shorthand for a viscous, binding liquid or the "mercurial glue" that holds the matter together</note>, knowing that as many times as you soak the ash, it must be dried just as many times, and moistened again, until its color turns into that which you seek. 

Beyond these things, know that the perfection of this precious stone lies in managing it with a third part of the medicine, while keeping two parts back to moisten it in turns, cooking it until the proper color is reached. Let the fire be more intense than the first, until the matter flows like wax—which, when it is dried, holds itself together. Cook it, therefore, until it drinks the **glue of gold** <note>original: "colla auri"; likely referring to *chrysocolla*, a material used in soldering gold, but here used metaphorically for the final bonding of the stone's elements</note>, and when it is dried...

# THE ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

...Look, children of doctrine, how painters cannot paint with their colors until they turn them into ashes and pulverize them. Similarly, philosophers often cannot compose medicines for their sick unless the ingredients are broken and pulverized. Because if you manage that ash subtly, many things will proceed from it, for the reason that **copper** <term>copper: original Latin "aes"; in alchemy, this rarely refers to common copper but rather to the "Philosophical Copper" or the base metallic body chosen for the work.</term>, like a man, has a body and a spirit. Man’s breathing is from the air; similarly, copper, having breathed in moisture, receives life and is multiplied and increased like all other things. 

And for this reason, the philosophers said that when copper is burned, it becomes better than it was before. Furthermore, this copper of ours, when it is first cooked, becomes water; then, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened, until it becomes a stone surpassing every metal. Afterward, it is broken, soaked, and roasted with a more intense fire until it is colored and becomes like *burnt blood* <note>original: "combusto sanguini similis"; a stage in the alchemical process where the matter takes on a deep red hue, often called the "Rubedo" or Reddening.</note>; then place the coins <note>original: "nummos"; likely referring to the small pieces of metal or the specific weights of the material being transformed.</note> into it, and it dyes them into gold. 

For just as sperm is not made from blood unless it is diligently cooked in the liver <note>original: "epate"; refers to the medieval physiological belief that the liver was the site of "concoction" or the refining of bodily fluids.</note>, so our work is by no means a **tincture** <term>tincture: a substance capable of "staining" or transforming the inner nature and color of a base metal into a noble one.</term> unless it is diligently cooked until it becomes powder, and thus through **putrefaction** the sperm itself is made spiritual in its effect. For then the color which you have sought will be found, and not otherwise.

**NICARUS** <note>Another speaker in this philosophical assembly; his name, like many in the Turba, may be a corrupted version of a Greek or Arabic name.</note> says: I command those who come after us to take the gold which they wish to multiply and reno- <meta>catchword: uare (to renew)</meta>

**ZEUMON** says: The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. ### THE PHILOSOPHERS

That which is precious is not made without that which is vile, nor that which is vile without that which is precious. Therefore, it behooves you to follow the sayings of the elders, who said: Nothing else is of use to you except to sublime the water and the vapor. For when you see those two purified natures become water, and the entire body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In medieval alchemy, this does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but to a mysterious "mother-substance" or raw mineral mass believed to contain the seed of gold.</term> melted into water, then certainly all things are vapor; by right, then the vapor contains its companion—that is, water [contains] water.

Wherefore the philosophers named both "vapor," because they are united together in **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the stage of the "Great Work" where the material decomposes and turns black, signifying the death of its old form before a new one can be born.</term> and **decoction** <term>decoctio: the process of prolonged heating or "boiling" the substance to refine it.</term>, and one contains the other so that it does not flee <note>In alchemical texts, a substance that "flees" is volatile and evaporates; the goal is to "fix" it so it remains stable under heat.</note>. Therefore, they become permanent. For the hidden nature is congealed in the body, and its color is changed, and it casts off its own nature, and is bound so that it does not flee. 

If **blackness** <term>nigredo: the black stage, considered the most difficult and essential part of the transformation.</term> appears, it is out of sickness, and it dies in putrefaction, and becomes **rust** <note>original: "rubigo"; here referring to a reddish or orange oxidation that signals the transition from the black stage toward the final red stage.</note>, and then by the law of nature it does not flee, because it has dismissed the servitude of flight, and the nature has been made free, following its spouse, adorning him with its color and beauty—not as it had done before, but having taken up the **gold coin** <note>original: "nummo aureo"; a metaphor for the "solar" or golden principle that provides the final perfection and life to the substance.</note>, it gives him life. 

And the philosophers have called this nature the **spirit** and the **soul**. Furthermore, they said that the moist spirit is black, yet lacking in defilement. And just as in man there is humidity and dryness, so in our work there is nothing else than vapor and water. For this reason, the ancients said o-

...Therefore he shall be patient of spirit <note>original: "longanimis"; implying the steadfast and enduring temperament required for the years of labor in alchemical practice.</note>, and will freely enjoy the fruits of patience; such a man shall walk in the just path of **this art** <term>this art: Alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" (Ars Magna) of transmuting matter and soul.</term>. **ACTOMANUS** says: The Philosophers have very frequently discussed rust <note>original: "rubigine"; in alchemy, this refers to "rubedo" or the reddening of the matter, the final stage of the Great Work</note>. **MUNDUS** says: Enough has been said about rust; therefore, I shall speak about the poison <note>original: "veneno"; here, "poison" does not mean a toxin, but rather a "penetrating medicine" or the transformative elixir that "attacks" and changes the nature of base metals</note>. The poison is not a physical body, because the subtle spirits have made it a thin spirit itself; they have tinted the body and turned it into poison. The philosophers assert that this poison tints every body: and for this reason, they believe that whoever turns gold into poison has already reached his goal; but he who has not, has achieved nothing. But I say that unless you thin these things with fire, until those things rise like spirits, you have as yet perfected nothing.

...[most] great: because only sulfur whitens copper. You investigators of this art must also be informed that this sulfur could not whiten the copper until it was itself whitened in the prior work; for the habit of this sulfur is to **flee** <term>flee|To volatilize or evaporate when exposed to heat; a major challenge for early chemists was keeping "spirits" from escaping the vessel.</term>. Therefore, when its thick bodies flee and the vapor is **sublimated** <term>sublimated|The process where a substance is heated until it becomes a gas and then cools back into a solid on the upper part of the vessel, effectively purifying it.</term>, then you must contain it with another **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury.</note> of its own kind so that it does not flee. This happens as soon as the quicksilver and the copper itself are joined. For then they often mutually dissolve and conceive, and do not allow [the spirit] to flee, but both become quicksilver. And so, this which at first was neither copper nor quicksilver, was nevertheless made [into one] by the mixture of quicksilver: which, being added to the quicksilver, contains the former quicksilver that used to flee. Wherefore the philosophers said:

> **Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs.** <note>original: "Sulphura sulphuribus continentur." This is a famous alchemical axiom suggesting that like-substances must be used to stabilize or "fix" one another.</note>

Know further that sulfurs dye, and then undoubtedly flee, unless they are joined to quicksilver of their own kind. Therefore, do not think that this thing which dyes and then flees is the **coin** <note>original: "nummus"; a metaphor used for the alchemical stone or its base material.</note> of the common people; rather, the philosophers' intention is the "coin" which, unless it is mixed with the white or the red (which is quicksilver of its own kind), will undoubtedly flee. I command you, therefore, to mix quicksilver with quicksilver, until they become one and the same clean water, composed of the two. This, therefore, is the greatest **secret** <note>original: "arcanum".</note>,

**EXIMENUS** said: The philosophers have named our philosophy and our work by many and almost all the names of metals; but however they may call it, they always signify the **water** itself. This water, when placed with its substances in its vessel, prevents the substances from being burned; and the more the substances themselves are seized by flame, the more they are hidden in the depths of the water, lest they be harmed by the heat of the fire. Now the water receives them into its vessel and repels the flame of the fire from them. And so, once the substances are diligently ground with the water, the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia|A recurring term in early alchemy, likely referring to a "spirit" or vaporous substance that rises during heating, or the "hidden soul" of the metal.</term> ascends, and thereafter leads the work to its true end solely through the **imbibition** <term>imbibition|The process of repeatedly soaking a dry substance in a liquid until it has absorbed it completely, often used to "nourish" the alchemical stone.</term> of the water.

For all the philosophers have said: He who is able to turn gold into rust has already found the purpose of the **poison** <note>original: "veneni"; in alchemical texts, "poison" or "venom" often refers to the potent, transformative elixir or a powerful mercurial solvent.</note>; but he who cannot do this has achieved nothing.

# THE ASSEMBLY

Quicksilver <note>original: "vivum"; short for *argentum vivum*</note> appears white to the sight, but when smoke <note>vapor or fumes from the fire</note> reaches it, it turns into red and becomes **Cambar**, which is to say, poison. And for this reason, the ancients also treated much concerning **sublimation** <term>Sublimation|The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then collects again as a solid in the upper part of the vessel; used here to separate the pure spirit from the "dross."</term>: because unless the matter is strongly ground by the fire, **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia|An alchemical term for the volatile spirit, soul, or "cloud" that rises during heating.</term> will not ascend, which **Hermes** intended to suggest when he said:
> Sift the things you know, and liquefy them more highly.

**BODillus** <note>One of the legendary sages in the Turba Philosophorum, a text composed of a fictional debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> said: All you disciples should know that nothing useful is made from the elements without the mixing of the male and the female, and the governance of heat: because the seed <term>seed|sperma; in alchemy, the vital essence or the combination of "Sulfur" and "Mercury" that begins the Great Work.</term> is generated from blood and desire. For when the man is joined with the woman, the seed is nourished by the moisture of the womb, and by the wetting blood, and by heat; the offspring <note>original: "partus"</note> is formed in forty nights. For if the moisture of the womb and the heat were not present, the seed would not remain, nor would the fetus be completed. God, however, ordained that blood and heat to nourish the seed until He might extract it at His will. 

But the fetus, once extracted, is nourished only by milk <note>original: "lacte"; often refers to the "Virgin's Milk" or the white liquid used in the whitening stage (albedo) of alchemy.</note> and by fire—on its own and gradually while it is small—and the more it is "burned" as the bones are strengthened, the more it is led into youth: arriving at which state, it is sufficient for itself. 

Thus, therefore, you must act in this art. And know that without heat nothing is ever generated, and that a bath of intense heat causes [the work] to perish; if indeed it is cold, it flees; but if it is temperate, it becomes suitable and pleasant for the body. Wherefore they become light and are nourished, and the flesh is increased.

"Featherless" refers to the "fixed" or solid state, while "flying with feathers" refers to the "volatile" or gaseous state achieved during sublimation.</note> and if you call it water, you speak the truth: if you deny it is water, you have not denied falsely. <note>This refers to the <term>mercurial|the fluid, metallic principle</term> nature of the substance, which looks like liquid but behaves differently than common water.</note> Do not, therefore, be deceived by the countless number of names, for it is dead, even while it lives. But hold it for certain, that it is a thing to which nothing foreign is added nor introduced. <note>A core alchemical principle: the Work must be completed using only its own internal components, without outside additives.</note> Therefore, seek out its companion, and introduce nothing foreign to it, and let men multiply its names:

-> children would laugh at <-
-> our wisdom. <-
<note>original: "sapientiam nostram pueri riderent"; the author suggests that the secret of alchemy is so simple in its essence that if it were stated plainly, the uninitiated or "children" would mock its simplicity. # THE PRINTER
## To the Reader.

*It has pleased us, kind Reader, so that we might look out for your benefit, to also include another copy of the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turbæ exemplar"; referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting between ancient sages</note> which we had in our possession, not so much because of a different order of contents, but rather for the variety of opinions and the names of the philosophers.* *For it happens that in the other volume, the same idea may be expressed with a different meaning, in different words, and attributed to another author; this is done so that in a matter of such great importance you may not go astray, but instead may follow in your **operations** <note>alchemical laboratory processes or experiments</note> whichever version appeals to you more.* *Farewell; and if you derive any benefit from this, you shall attribute it to that most distinguished and excellent Physician, Master William Rascalon of Worms <note>William Rascalon (Guilielmus Rascalonus) was a 16th-century physician from Worms, Germany, who provided the manuscripts for this edition</note>, through whose generosity we obtained these copies.*

THESE are the opinions of the Wise, collected in the third Pythagorean Synod <note>original: "Synodo Pythagorica"; referring to a legendary gathering of ancient sages under the leadership or tradition of Pythagoras</note>: In which it is said that the philosopher Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a recurring legendary master in alchemical literature, sometimes identified with Aristaios</note> gathered the disciples of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> and the elders of the Wise, and he commanded each one to bring forward something in their midst concerning the vegetable stone <note>original: "lapide vegetabili"; in alchemy, the "vegetable stone" refers to the life-giving or growing principle of the Great Work, often associated with the soul or the spirit of mercury</note>, so that the sacred art might become known to posterity: and so that those who had applied their minds to grasping it might be led to the path of truth. ## DOCTRINE II.

**Ysindrus** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name, possibly Hesiod or Anaximenes, as this text often distorts classical names</note>. I praise the aerial things, for the work itself is refined by air. When it is thickened, it becomes thin; when it is heated, it becomes cold. Its thickness <term>thickness: (Latin: *spissitudo*) in this context refers to density or the materialization of a substance from a spirit-like state</term> occurs when it is dispersed in the heavens because of the sun’s distance. But its thinness occurs when, the sun being high, the air melts and becomes clear. It happens similarly in the temperament of Spring, in the distinction of a season that is neither hot nor cold. For according to the change of the established arrangement, to change the divisions of the year, winter is changed: therefore the air is thickened then, when the sun is moved far away from it. But when the air becomes thin, the sun is near; and when it is near, its heat reaches humanity.

## STATEMENT X

EXIMENUS <note>original: *Eximenus*; likely a corruption of the name Anaximenes, the Pre-Socratic philosopher</note>. After this, govern the substance and mix in the **soul of gold** <note>the "soul" (anima) usually refers to the concentrated red essence or the coloring principle of gold</note> and cook it until it becomes a red Ethelia. Grind this with patience, and do not let it weary you to moisten it with the water that came out of it—which is permanent—until it becomes red. For this is the **burnt copper** <note>original: *æs combustum*</note>, the flower of gold, and the **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance added to the alchemical "dough" to "leaven" the mass and direct its transformation toward the nature of gold or silver</term>. Process this with the permanent water, then dry it until it becomes a powder and is stripped of all moisture.

### THE TWELFTH OPINION

**PARMENIDES** <note>A famous pre-Socratic Greek philosopher, here cast as one of the authoritative masters in the alchemical assembly</note>: Know that the **envious ones** <term>the envious: a common alchemical term for previous authors who intentionally used confusing metaphors to hide secrets from the "unworthy" or uninitiated</term> have written in many ways concerning waters, broths, bodies, and metals, in order to deceive those seeking this knowledge. Therefore, set these things aside, and make gold and coins from this copper of ours; and understand that copper or lead is used for its fatness or blackness, and tin is used for its ease of melting.

[Perfec]t <note>Continuing from the previous page: "perfect the burnt copper"</note> it, knowing that unless you direct the natures of truth and their **combinations** <note>original: *complexiones*; referring to the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance</note>, and join blood-like things with blood-like things, you achieve nothing. Indeed, natures meet their own natures, and follow them, and rejoice in them, and when they rot, they are born. For Nature is governed, and in the same way she fell, she is raised up; and while she is destroyed, she is turned into dust and reduced to nothing: then she is reborn and renewed.

Strive, therefore, to know what it is that makes her rot and what renews her, and what its flavor is, and what its distance and proximity are, and how friendship arises after enmity, and how corruption and generation occur, and how those natures embrace each other, and how they become harmonious in a gentle fire.

Having noted and perceived these things, apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of these stated qualities, do not approach the work; for it is entirely harmful, bringing misfortune and sorrow. In this single word the **whole work** <note>original: *totum opus*; the Great Work or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note> is contained.

### FIFTEENTH OPINION

**ASSUBERES:** I say that sulphurs are contained by sulphurs, and moisture by moisture. They hinted at this when they said: "it is best that a small force of sulfur burns a strong body."

Therefore they venerate this substance and describe it in their books, saying: "This vinegar burns bodies, turns them into ash, and whitens them." If it is cooked well and stripped of its blackness, it will become a stone and a most white **coin** <note>original: *nummus*; a common alchemical metaphor for the perfected matter of the "White Work" (silver).</note>. Therefore, cook it until it is broken down; then dissolve it and place it in seawater. Know that the beginning of this work is **whitening** <note>original: *dealbatio*; the albedo stage of the Great Work.</note>, which is followed by **redness** <note>original: *rubor*; the rubedo, or final stage.</note>. Afterward, the perfection of the body is achieved through vinegar.

I have investigated this vinegar through long labor; finally, by the will of God Most High, I saw one nature which is more powerful, noble, and stronger than all natures. This nature is nothing other than clean water, **sharpest vinegar** <note>original: *acetum acerrimum*.</note>, and **permanent water** <note>original: *aqua permanens*; an indestructible, spiritualized solvent central to alchemical theory.</note>, which illuminates all bodies and provides light to all who read our books.

->PROPOSITION XVII<-

**SOCRATES** <note>Socrates appears here not as the historical philosopher, but as a legendary authority within the alchemical tradition of the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> said: Know, sons of the doctrine, that without **lead** <note>original: *plumbum*; often referred to as "Saturn," lead was considered the base starting material that contained the hidden "gold" of the philosophers.</note> no **dyeing** <note>original: *tinctura*; the process of transforming or "coloring" base metals into gold or silver.</note> occurs, and that the power of the work is within it. Do you not see, said Her- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; this is likely a reference to **Hermes** Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note>

## STATEMENT XVIII

**ZENON**. You have already taught the doctrine of how to create the white; what now of the red? I say that you cannot make the red unless you first strive to **whiten** <note>referring to *albedo*, the stage of purification where the matter becomes white, which must precede the final red stage, or *rubedo*.</note>: because the two natures are nothing other than the white and the red. Whiten the red, therefore, and turn the white into red, knowing that the year is divided into four seasons. The first season is of a cold nature: and it is **winter**. The second is of an airy nature: and it is **spring**. The third season is of a fiery nature: and it is **summer**. The fourth is **autumn**, in which the fruits are ripened.

# THE TURBA

### STATEMENT XXX

CUSTOS <note>The name means "Guardian." Of these two, therefore, the nature is one, and a closeness is mixed between them; if this were not so, they would not combine so quickly, nor would they contain one another, nor become one.

It is extracted in this way: grind it, and place it in the water seven times until it drinks all the moisture and receives the power to withstand the battle of the fire; and then it is called **rust** <note>original: *rubigo*; in alchemical philosophy, "rust" often represents the external impurity that must be refined to reveal the inner "gold."</note>. Therefore, rot it <term>rot: or 'putrefy'; the process of breaking down a substance through moisture and gentle heat to release its essence.</term> diligently until it becomes a **spiritual powder** in the color of dried blood; let the power of the fire bring forth this color until it is clothed in an unchanging hue.

### STATEMENT XXXVII.

**ZEUNON.** The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. That which we seek is sold publicly at a very low price, and if it were known, the merchants would not sell even the slightest bit of it. The Philosophers, however, have honored this vile and discarded thing, and have called it by every name: they said that it is a **stone and yet not a stone** <note>A famous alchemical paradox signifying that the "Philosopher's Stone" is a substance found everywhere but recognized by few.</note>, and that it is the **gum of Scotland** <note>original: *guma Scotiæ*; likely a corruption of *gummi Scythiae* (gum of Scythia) or a symbolic term for a sticky, resinous state of the matter during transformation.</note>. For this reason, the philosophers hid the power of this poison, because within it is the spirit you seek, which performs the tinting.

<summary>Barsenites and Zeunon discuss the extraction of a transformative "spirit" from common or "vile" substances like Corfusle or a low-priced material, emphasizing the need for repeated cooking and purification until a blood-red, stable color is achieved.</summary>

### PROPOSITION XLII.

**EFISTES** <note>This name likely refers to a participant in the assembly, possibly a corruption of a Greek name like Epistemon.</note> Pay attention, sons of doctrine, to what Hermes, the head of the Philosophers, said when he taught how to mix the natures. Do this many times until two parts of the water perish, and the colors appear to you. And know that the whitening <note>original: "dealbatio". A key stage in the Great Work where the material is purified to a white state.</note> does not happen except by cooking, and for that reason, the process is repeated by grinding and soaking very frequently. I command, however, that you do not pour the water all at once, lest the **Ysir** <term>Ysir: A variant of Yxir (Elixir), the transformative powder or catalyst.</term> be submerged: but pour it in little by little, grind, dry, and do this quite often, until they become water. And the philosophers said: Once the water is assimilated <note>original: "simitata". Likely a technical term for the water being fully absorbed or unified with the solid.</note>, leave it until it is fixed below. This means, as the moisture dries up and is turned into powder in its glass vessel, leave it for forty days until it brings forth various colors. By this governance <note>original: "regimine". The method of managing heat and time.</note> bodies become spirits, and hot spirits are made that can tint <note>original: "tingunt". To 'tint' or 'dye' in alchemy means to successfully project the elixir onto a base metal to transform its color and nature into gold or silver.</note>.

### PROPOSITION LXIII.

**ADMION** <note>A speaker in the Assembly, likely a Latinized version of a Greek or Arabic name.</note> says: Wise men, you cannot reach the benefit of the art without a prolonged and continuous regimen <term>regimen: The controlled process of heating, timing, and chemical treatment required to transform the material.</term>. Therefore, he who is patient in the regimen will enter the art; but he who is not, let him not read our propositions, because they will cause him harm once read. And so the Master said: He who labors in reading our books, and devotes himself to them, not entangled in various thoughts, and prays to God, shall reign in a kingdom until he dies. For what is sought is not of little value, but is a gift of God; for this reason, there is need for patience and labor. For we see that he who grafts trees hopes for fruit in time; he who sows, reaps after months.

Watch therefore and learn to mix, to cook, to simulate <note>original: "simulare". In alchemical context, this often refers to "imitating" the natural process or achieving a specific appearance.</note>, to roast, to heat, to whiten <note>original: "dealbare". The stage of Albedo, or purification.</note>, to grind, to level the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia: A term derived from the Greek word for "vapor" or "spirit," referring to the volatile substance that rises during sublimation.</term>, and to make the rust <note>original: "rubiginem". A reference to the reddening or "Rubedo" stage, the final part of the process.</note>, and finally to dye. These are many names, yet the regimen is one: but the decoction <term>decoction: The process of boiling or heating a substance in liquid to extract its essence or transform it.</term> is continuous, for which reason they have repeated it often, so that the compound may be ground and the cooking may be done perpetually; do not let the labor weary you. The goal, however, is that you adjust the temperaments <note>original: "complexiones". The balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>; then cook them in many ways, saturate the decoctions, and cook until the spirits become impalpable <note>original: "impalpabiles". So finely ground or refined that they cannot be felt by touch.</note>. And you shall see **Ysir** <term>Ysir: A variant of Yxir (Elixir), the transformative catalyst or "Stone."</term> clothed in a royal garment, and turned into a Tyrian color <note>Tyrian color: A deep purple or crimson dye, symbolizing the successful completion of the Great Work.</note>; then you will understand the sayings of the Philosophers.

### PROPOSITION XLIV.

**LARGUS** <note>A speaker in the Assembly; the name translates to "Bountiful" or "Abundant."</note> says: The Copper <note>original: "Æs." In alchemy, this rarely refers to the common metal, but rather a "philosophical" copper or the base material of the Great Work.</note> of which the first masters spoke is not copper, nor the tin of the common people; but rather it is our "body," which must be mixed with the body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In alchemical terms, this is not the modern chemical magnesium, but a "magnetic" or "attractive" primal matter, often described as a white or black earth that "draws" the spirit.</term>, so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. Then, that stone is ground in a vessel with nitre water <note>original: "aqua nitri." A solution of saltpeter or a similar salty, acidic solvent.</note>, and it is liquefied until it is broken down. It is necessary, however, for you to have a water which, the more it is cooked, the more it thickens, until it acquires a rust <note>original: "rubiginem." Cook this, and grind it with Egyptian vinegar <term>Egyptian vinegar: An alchemical term for a highly potent, distilled solvent or acid capable of "mortifying" metals.</term>.

### PROPOSITION XLV.

**CADMON**. I signal to those who come after us that the round thing <note>original: "rotundum." The method of extraction is this: take one part of copper and three parts of permanent water <term>permanent water: Often referring to "mercury of the philosophers," a liquid that does not wet the hands and acts as a universal solvent.</term>; then let them be mixed and cooked until they thicken and become a single stone, of which the philosophers have said: Take one part of the sincere body and three parts of the copper of **Magnesia**; then mix them with "straight masculine vinegar" <note>original: "aceto recto masculino." A symbolic name for a strong, "active" acid.</note> mixed with earth, cover the vessel, and observe what is inside, and cook it continually until they become earth.

But this concerns the **Second Work** <note>The alchemical process was often divided into stages; the "First Work" usually involves the preparation and purification of the raw matter, while the "Second Work" focuses on the union and perfection of the substance.</note>; of the first I shall say a few things: Provoke a war between the **copper** <note>original: "æs." But the quicksilver, conceiving the copper, is congealed into earth. 

Therefore, provoke the battle and destroy the body of the copper until it becomes dust. Join the male to the female (which is made from vapor) and the quicksilver, until the male and female become **Etheel** <term>Etheel: A term derived from the Arabic "al-ithil," referring to a sublimated or spiritualized substance that has been purged of its dross.</term>. For he who turns them into spirit through **Etheel**, then makes them red, tints every body; because when the body is ground diligently, a clean soul—spiritual and sublime—is extracted from it, which tints every body; and it is the **sulfur of nature**, which is called by various names.

## SENTENCE XLVIII.

**Mosius** <note>original: *Mosius*. Likely a corruption of "Moses" or a specific sage named in the *Turba Philosophorum* tradition.</note> said: This one thing that has been mentioned so often, the philosophers have called by many names: sometimes by two names, and occasionally even by three. Now I shall tell you what it is: the first is that **fiery** thing; the second is the **composite** within it; and the third is the **water of sulfur**, by which the "one" is washed, ground down, and governed until it is completed. And this is what the philosopher hinted at when he said: The **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Latin *argentum vivum*, or mercury.</term> that tinges gold is the quicksilver of **Cambar** <term>Cambar: A specialized alchemical term, here identified with Magnesia, but often associated with red lead or a specific state of the "living" metal.</term>. 

Nevertheless, the philosophers distinguish and say: sometimes it is Cambar, sometimes it is **orpiment** <term>Orpiment: Latin *auripigmentum*. A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral prized by alchemists for its golden color and volatility.</term>, but you must understand it thus: The quicksilver of Cambar is **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In alchemy, this is not modern magnesium, but the "chaos" or "prime matter"—a mystical substance containing the seeds of all metals.</term>. The quicksilver of the late stage, however, is the orpiment or the **sulfur** that ascends from the mixed composite. 

Therefore, you must mix that thick substance with the **fiery poison** <note>original: *veneno igneo*. This refers to a corrosive or highly reactive substance, likely an acid or a sharp mineral vapor, used to break down the "body" of the metal.</note>, and putrefy it, and diligently grind it until it becomes a **spirit** within another hidden spirit; and then the **tincture** <note>The final substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold.</note> is made, which tinges everything you wish.

## PROPOSITION LVI.

**YS Imidrus** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic name, common in alchemical texts to lend authority to the discourse.</note>. Enough and more has been treated regarding the governance of the air and the moist spirit; I shall now complete what was omitted. It must therefore be known that the philosophers have assigned many names to it. Sometimes it is called the **water of Ethelia** <term>Ethelia: From the Greek *aithalē*, meaning vapor or soot. In alchemy, it refers to a sublimated substance or a spiritualized vapor.</term>, of which mention was made above; when this water is whitened, it whitens and dyes. It is also called by them the **flower of gold**, and before it dyes or reaches this end, it is called **copper** <note>original: *æs*. While *æs* often means bronze or copper, in alchemy it refers to the 'base' state of the metal before transformation.</note>. 

Truly, when it is joined with four things which the Sages have called **fermented urines** <note>A common alchemical code (deck-name) for specific chemical solutions or salts used to trigger a reaction.</note>, they call it the **Heart**, and the **glue of gold**. Mercury, viewed here as a substance 'extracted by men' through their art, rather than just found in nature.</term> extracted by men, from which and with which all things are made. It is said to be the **mundane water** <note>original: *aqua mundana*. Literally 'water of the world,' implying a universal solvent or primary matter.</note> which deletes every shadow. 

And it must be known that when this quicksilver extracted by men is whitened, it becomes **sulfur**, which is contained by sulfur; it is a **poison** that is likened to shining marble. This the philosophers have called **Ethelia**, and **Orpiment** <term>Orpiment: Latin *Auri pigmentum*. Here referring to realgar (red arsenic sulfide), often associated with the 'red' stage of the work.</term>. From this, the **tincture** and the pure spirit ascend by a slow fire, and from this, the flower is sublimated. 

This entire secret is nothing other than quicksilver extracted by men—that is, through the agency of men. Furthermore, it must be known that to whiten the **secret copper** <note>original: *arcanum æs*. The hidden or inner essence of the base metal being worked upon.</note> does not...

### PROPOSITION 59

**Anaxagoras**. Take the burnt fugitive <note>original: *combustum fugiens*. This refers to a volatile spirit that has been subjected to fire.</note>, which lacks a body, and give it a body. **Constans**. What have we to do with the envious and their treatises? ### PROPOSITION LXIV <note>original: *Sententia LXIIII*. In this context, a "sententia" is a formal proposition or aphorism delivered by one of the sages in the assembly.</note>

**BALGUS.** Someone described the fruit of that art of Tulleas <note>original: *Tulleas*. This refers to a specific sage or authority mentioned within the *Turba Philosophorum*, a foundational alchemical text.</note>, and in a wonderful way he began to teach me, saying: that its operation is found without labor. And when he began to teach concerning its growth and construction, he spoke these things: "Take that tree, and build for it a **round and dark house** <note>The "round house" is a metaphorical description of the alchemical vessel, such as a retort or a flask, which is sealed to contain the transformation.</note>, surrounded by dew, and place in it an **old man** <term>Old man: Latin *veterem hominem*. I say to you in truth, that that old man does not cease to eat of the fruit of that tree, until he **becomes young again**. O how wonderful is that tree, which by its fruits pours the soul into a youthful body, and converts the **father into the son**." <note>The conversion of "father into son" symbolizes the transmutation of the original, "aged" base metal into a "new," refined substance, such as gold or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

Historically used to describe substances used for soldering gold, here a metaphor for the agent that fixes the transformation.</note>, **red sulfur**, and **orpiment** <note>original: *auripigmentum*. A golden-yellow mineral (arsenic trisulfide), used here as a symbolic name for a stage of the work.</note>. However, while it remains raw, it is called lead...

### PROPOSITION LXXVIII.

**AGMON**. As a corollary I say, that he who does not **liquefy and coagulate** <term>liquefy and coagulate <note>original: *liquefacit & coagulat*. This refers to the fundamental alchemical principle of *Solve et Coagula*: dissolving a substance to its base components and then recombining them into a higher form.</note></term>, errs in many ways. Therefore, **blacken** <note>This refers to the *Nigredo* stage, the first step in the Great Work, symbolizing death and the breakdown of matter.</note> the earth, and separate its soul and water, and afterwards **whiten** it <note>This refers to the *Albedo* stage, the second step of the process, representing purification and the "washing" of the matter.</note>, and you will find what you seek. I also tell you, that he who blackens the earth and dissolves the white with fire, until it becomes like a **naked sword** <note>original: *gladius denudatus*. Likely referring to the brilliant, sharp, or silver-like metallic luster of the purified substance.</note>, and who introduces the soul to that which was previously completely whitened, and **fixes** <term>fixes <note>original: *figit*. In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat.</note></term> the whole with a **consuming fire** <note>original: *tabido igne*. Often implies a slow, melting heat that transforms the substance.</note> after it has been liquefied—that man deserves to be called happy and to be exalted above the circles of the world.

We do not doubt that this is enough for the **sons of doctrine** <note>A traditional term for students and practitioners initiated into the secrets of the alchemical art.</note> regarding the revelation of our **stone** <term>stone <note>original: *lapidis*. The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the work, which is not a literal rock but a perfected substance.</note></term>, whose powers cannot be corrupted. If it is placed in fire, its power is increased; if you wish to **dissolve** it, it will be dissolved; if to **coagulate**, it will be coagulated. No one can be without it, and everyone needs it. And though it has many names, it is nonetheless known by a single name, and where the father is, there it is **hidden** <note>original: *cælatur*. This can mean 'hidden', 'carved', or 'sealed'.</note>. It is also a **stone and not a stone** <note>A classic alchemical paradox indicating that the material has physical form but divine or spiritual properties.</note>, spirit and soul and body. It is white, volatile, hollow, and **lacking hair** <note>original: *pilis carens*. A cryptic description used in the *Turba* to describe a smooth, refined state of matter or perhaps the appearance of mercury.</note>, which no one can touch with their tongue when cooled without injury. If you make it fly, it flies; and if you say it is water, you speak the truth; and if you say it is not water, you speak a falsehood. Not so—

# ALLEGORIES UPON THE book of the Turba.

The allegories upon the book of the **Turba** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*. This is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a gathering of philosophers discussing the secrets of nature.</note> begin. And first, concerning **man**.

Take a man, shave him, and draw <note>original: *trahe*. In this context, it implies a process of grinding, rubbing, or dragging the substance across a surface to break it down.</note> him over a stone or a metal plate until his body dies and its **density** <note>original: *spissitudo*. In alchemy, this refers to the solid, coarse, material state of a substance before it is purified or vaporized.</note> vanishes. Know for certain that once it has lost its density, it will become **spiritual**; afterward, return its soul to it. Next, place it in a bath for forty days so that, just as a seed dies in the womb—which is truly the beginning of nature's **regeneration**—a new creation may rise and the goal may be achieved.

Take a **bull** with its flesh and blood, its horns and its hooves, and turn it into water. Mix it with its blood and process the whole; afterward, roast it until it turns red. Afterward, turn the **copper** <note>original: *æs*. While this literally means copper or bronze, in alchemy it often refers to the "base" metal or the "body" of the material being transformed.</note> into divine tinctures.

Take a **Cock**, crowned with a red crest, and while it is alive, strip it of its feathers. Then, place its head in a glass vessel and keep it there for an hour. Afterward, store the cock again and process it until it is softened and purified, and spread it upon marble. Then, with the feathers having been removed from it, process and shear it very strongly. Then, leave it in **horse dung** <note>original: *equorum fimo*. Decaying horse dung was a standard laboratory tool for alchemists, used to provide a gentle, steady, and natural heat for fermentation or digestion.</note> until it grows feathers again. And when you hear that cock crowing like a living cock, know that you have walked the right path.

# ON THE TURBA <note>original: *Super Turbam*. This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a foundational text in the Latin alchemical tradition.</note>

Take a **viper**, which is called *de rexa* <note>original: *de rexa*. Likely a technical or regional name for a specific type of snake, used here as an alchemical symbol for a volatile substance.</note>, and deprive it of its head and tail; in these two places its venom liquefies, from which the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*. In alchemy, the "spirit" is the volatile, vaporous essence of a substance that can be released through heat.</note> proceeds. Therefore, divide the head and the tail, and store each by itself in a glass vessel. Take the remaining body and cook it over a slow fire until the flesh is separated from the bones. And afterward, place the flesh upon a metal plate, and process it until the body is turned into **spirit**, and its **flexibility** <note>original: *flexibilitas*. This refers to the physical "toughness" or "oiliness" of the matter; the alchemist seeks to remove this to reach a dry, crystalline, or "spiritual" state.</note> is taken away from it. 

For that which is flexible cannot be refined. Then, join it to its head and grind it together until the body [is fully processed], so long as any flexibility remains within it. Dry a body of this kind in the sun or by the fire, so that you may see what you seek. Once this is completed, know that you have a **body penetrating bodies**, and a **nature containing nature**, and a **nature rejoicing in nature** <note>This triad—nature containing nature, nature overcoming nature, and nature rejoicing in nature—is one of the oldest and most famous axioms in alchemy, traditionally attributed to Bolos of Mendes.</note>, which is called the **perfection of the philosophers’ theriac** <term>theriac: originally a medicinal "universal antidote" against poison, used here to describe the alchemical Elixir that "cures" base metals into gold.</term>.

There is in the sea a **round fish**, lacking bones and skin, and it possesses within itself a fatness—a wonderful virtue—which, if it be cooked over a slow fire until its fatness and moisture completely depart, and afterwards is ground very strongly and soaked with seawater until it shines; then let it be buried for a week, and afterward let it be whitened by roasting. And when it has been well whitened, and its water restored to it: afterward let it be soaked in its own moisture; then, after the soaking in moisture, let it be roasted until it appears **yellow** <note>original: *citrinus*. The "citrinitas" or yellowing was a specific stage in the alchemical process, indicating the approach of the final "Red" work.</note>. It thus becomes the **philosophers’ eye-salve** <term>eye-salve: Latin *colirium*. An allegorical substance that allows the "eyes" of the practitioner to see the hidden truth of nature or completes the final tincture.</term>: with which, the eyes being anointed...

...the ancient secrets of the philosophers could easily be perceived. In the **moon of the sea** <note>original: *maris luna*. Men have **olives** from which they extract oil, and that oil is combustible. However, the **oil of the philosophers** is not extracted in this way. Nevertheless, its nature is combustible, and it always remains immobile. The method for making it is as follows: 

We take the olives, which we have kept clean and whole, and we grind them with their own water. Afterward, we boil them. Then, placing them in a damp place, we leave them there until they are almost dissolved, and until the oil is separated from its thick body. We also cause the dregs to descend to the bottom, the water to stand in the middle, and the oil to flow out on top. Afterward, we separate the water. Placing the matter upon a glowing metal plate, we soak it with its own water until its **flexibility** <note>original: *flexibilitatem*. Continued from the previous page, "flexibility" refers to the unrefined, oily state of the matter; the process aims to reach a state of "fixion" where the substance is stable and no longer "flexible" or volatile.</note>

# FROM THE VISION OF ARISLEUS THE PHILOSOPHER, AND THE ALLEGORIES OF THE SAGES.

## *RIDDLE I.*

When some of the more diligent disciples of the philosophers had gathered once again, along with Pythagoras—the most senior of whom was Arisleus, son of Abladius, followed by Paris, son of Belchiotus, Armenius, son of Archias, Meditatalus, Phaliseus, Echamisius, Parmenides, and Eximesias, son of Admirus—Auerca <note>Likely a speaker within the dialogue or a variation of a name found in the *Turba* manuscripts.</note> asked Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a central figure in alchemical lore, often interpreted as a latinization of a Greek or Arabic name; he serves as the primary narrator of the "Vision."</note> whether he could explain, by means of an example or a parable, how those seeking the **art** <note>original: *artis*. In this context, "the art" is Alchemy, the sacred process of material and spiritual transformation.</note> might be allowed to gather fruit from that **immortal tree** <note>A symbolic representation of the Philosopher's Stone or the completed Alchemical Work, which grants "fruit" in the form of wisdom and health.</note> which the aforementioned disciples and the others in the **Assembly** <note>original: *Turba*. This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages.</note> had described. 

And he replied, "I will certainly speak as best I can, though perhaps I may not satisfy your specific wish." 

And Pythagoras spoke again: "Speak, then, as aptly as you are able." 

And Arisleus said: "I saw myself and certain others from the Assembly riding toward the shores of the sea, and behold, I saw the inhabitants of the sea lying together with one another, yet nothing was born to them; and they were planting trees, yet they bore no fruit; and they were sowing seeds, yet nothing grew. And I said to them: 'What is the matter with you? ## RIDDLE II.
### Concerning the Stone.

In our sea, there is a **little round fish** <note>original: *pisciculus rotundus*. ### THE TRUMPETS <note>original: "BUCCINÆ," likely referring to the alchemical work *Clangor Buccinae* or "The Sound of the Trumpet."</note>

God in His essence does not die, except perhaps on the day of judgment. For the definition of death is the separation of that which is composed <note>i.e., death is the breaking apart of a compound into its individual parts</note>. However, in that which is not composed <note>simple or unitary substances</note>, there is no separation; hence there is no death or separation of the soul from the body [among simple beings]. For every compound made of two, three, or four components must necessarily be separated, which is the nature of death. And know that no compound lacking the element of fire eats, drinks, or sleeps. 

And how is it that since angels are created from fire, they do not eat? For it is said that fire is that which consumes <note>original: "comedit," literally eats; referring to the way a flame consumes fuel</note>. The answer is that simple fire <note>pure, celestial fire</note> does not consume, but rather "thick" or dense fire <note>material fire found on earth</note> does. For angels are not made from dense fire, but from the most subtle of the most subtle fire, which is simple. Therefore, having been created from this most subtle fire, they do not sleep, nor eat, nor drink.

Note that there are four primary qualities, namely heat, dryness, cold, and moisture. They are called the "primary qualities" because from them all the <term>elements: the four classical building blocks (Earth, Water, Air, Fire)</term> are composed; all things are "elemented" <note>given physical form through elements</note>, and all things are given a <term>complexion: the specific balance of these qualities that determines a being's nature or health</term>. And the elements themselves are made of these simple qualities. Therefore, they have the power to convert and change matter from one quality into another—sometimes into dry, sometimes into moist, sometimes into hot, and sometimes into cold—according to whether the division of nature is strengthened or weakened by the complexion of its elements. Common height is that which is manifest <note>The "manifest" refers to the outward, visible appearance of a substance.</note>; depth is that which is hidden <note>The "occult" or hidden inner nature of a substance, a core concept in alchemy where the interior often has opposite qualities to the exterior.</note>; and the width partakes in the middle of these. For this reason, if a body in its height <note>meaning its external/visible aspect</note> is *earthy*, then within it there is something *cold, dry, and melancholic, bitter, acidic, foul, black, and feminine*. And consequently, in its depth <note>its hidden/internal aspect</note> it is *airy, hot, moist, sanguine <note>meaning related to the humor of blood</note>, yellow, sweet, fragrant, and masculine*. And consequently, on the other side, it will be *fiery, hot, dry, and red*.

Each of them is composed of two primary qualities and no more: fire from heat and dryness, air from heat and moisture, water from cold and moisture, and earth from cold and dryness. Likewise, heat is the essential quality in fire, and dryness is its accidental <note>In this context, "essential" refers to the core nature of a thing, while "accidental" refers to a secondary characteristic that can be changed.</note> quality. In air, moisture is its essential quality, while heat is accidental. In water, moisture is its principal or essential quality, but coldness is its accidental quality. In earth, dryness is its principal or essential principle, and coldness is accidental. Furthermore, fire is properly hot and dry by nature. For heat is greater in a thing when it comes from its qualities than from its nature. Understand the other qualities of the elements in the same way.

Also, regarding the origin of the four elements, <note>original: "Mycretis," likely a corruption of the name Democritus or another ancient philosopher cited in alchemical texts</note> Mycretis says: Know that the earth was first water, then turned into stone and became rocky; water, however, was first air, then li—

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Likewise, concerning fire—that is, concerning "formal heat"—Eximidius says in the <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; The Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic sages.</note> *Assembly of the Philosophers*: The beginning of all things—that is, of created things—is a certain nature, and that nature is perpetual and first, "cooking" all things and leading them to their due form and species. Why does he say "perpetual and first"? Perhaps someone might understand this as referring to the First Essence <note>i.e., God or the act of Creation</note>, but that is not true. Rather, he says "perpetual," meaning spiritual, and "first," meaning the most worthy of all creatures existing within the elements; for otherwise, the statement would be false. It is this which digests and cooks all things, giving shape to the <term>natural heat: the innate warmth believed by ancients to drive biological growth and chemical transformation</term>, by which all things are led to their specific form and figure.

# -> THE CLANGING <-
<note>original: "CLANGOR"; likely referring to the title of the work, *Clangor Buccinae* (The Clangour of the Trumpet), symbolizing the loud proclamation of alchemical secrets.</note>

The sun does not heat the earth, nor does it imprint its power <note>original: "virtutem"; the inherent strength or essential quality of a celestial body</note> upon the earth except through the mediation of the moon, which among the other stars is more receptive to the sun's light and heat, acting as a medium between the sun and the earth. For this reason, as the philosophers say, there are two impediments that prevent one thing from imprinting its power upon another: namely, a remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is in the case of the sun and the earth, because the sun is far distant from the earth, and because the moon stands as a mediator there.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the same way, in our alchemical art, the sun does not perfect the <term>tincture: the transformative "dye" or essence capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> on its own except through the mediation of the moon. This is because it is distantly removed, as it has not yet reached that level of subtlety required to "tinge" or transform, and also because of those intermediate factors—namely, density and coarseness. For this reason, the moon is necessarily required there, so that she may refine the sun itself, making it rare and volatile, and separate out its impurity. For she, more than others, requires its light and nature among the other <gloss>planets, that is, metals</gloss>. <note>In traditional alchemy, the seven planets were directly linked to the seven metals: the Sun is Gold, the Moon is Silver, etc.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hence, in the *Epistle of the Sun to the Moon*, regarding the solar year when the moon begins to be joined with the sun in its thinness and to be illuminated by him, the sun first says: "In my sister the moon grows the degree of your wisdom, and not with any other of the servants..."

# -> THE SOUND OF THE TRUMPET <-

...the **prime matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the formless foundation of all physical reality.</note> of all things exists within each of them in the form of **Mercury** <term>the "Quicksilver" principle, representing the fluid, feminine, and passive potential of matter</term>. This matter is called the generative genus, a real being, and the material boundary of nature, in which nature takes up its material principles during the act of generation, for it is the primary subject in nature. 

For it is then that species are changed into a different form than they were before—yet it is not the "species" themselves <note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" is the abstract, unchanging essence or "blueprint" of a thing (like "silverness"), whereas the "individual" is the actual physical object you can touch.</note> that are changed, but rather the individuals of those species. This is because individuals are the objects of our physical senses, and they are, by their nature, subject to decay and corruption. 

Species, however, since they are universal, are not subject to physical actions; therefore, they are not corruptible in themselves. The species of silver—which is **silverness** <note>original: "argenteitas"</note>—does not change into the species of gold, which is **goldness** <note>original: "aureitas"</note>, nor the other way around. This is because true species cannot be changed; however, the individuals of a species can certainly be reduced back to their **prime matter**.

Because when the form of a thing has been corrupted and resolved into its prime matter, then a new form is necessarily introduced—for the **corruption of one is the generation of another** <note>A fundamental law of medieval science: when one thing "dies" or breaks down, its matter immediately becomes the "birth" of something else.</note>. But because matter can never be destroyed in such a way that it does not remain under some form, it follows that when one form of a metal is destroyed, another is immediately introduced. This occurs specifically through the transmutation of **Mercury** into **sulfur** <term>the "active" or "masculine" principle of heat and structure</term> for the sake of the operation we intend. Furthermore, every individual multiplies the form of its own species and not that of another, as **Aristotle** and **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully, a major figure in alchemical tradition.</note> say. It does not follow, therefore, that in the creation of the elements themselves, water was the first element, since the elements of air and fire existed prior, as was stated above. 

However, it is certainly true in our operation that among the visible elements which are seen and touched by us, water itself is the first element. Thus, in the **Art** <term>Alchemy</term>, there are only two formal elements that are seen and touched—namely, **water** and **earth**—though in potential <note>original: "virtualiter"; meaning their powers are present even if their forms are hidden.</note> there are four: namely, **air** within the water and **fire** within the earth.

For we call the "aqueous element" the humidity of the water itself; we call "air" the nature of the air itself; and "fire" we call 그 power it possesses by which it burns, **calcines** <term>reduces a metal to powder through heat</term>, and dissolves bodies. **Earth** is the dense and "gross" body itself. Thus, water and earth are seen and touched by us, while the other two are understood to be within these two. 

Therefore, it follows and is necessary that in the art of alchemy, metals must first be reduced into **Mercury**—that is, into **quicksilver**—which is the source-material and "sperm" <note>original: "sperma"; the generative principle or "seed" from which metals were believed to grow inside the earth.</note> of all metals. # -> THE TRUMPET <-

It is **Mercury** <term>Quicksilver</term>, boiled down and thickened within the womb of the earth by a **sulphurous heat** <note>Alchemical theory posits that all metals are born from the union of two principles: Sulphur (the active, "burning" principle) and Mercury (the passive, "liquid" principle).</note> that cooks it. According to the variety of this sulphur and its multiplication, different **metals** are procreated within the earth. For their **prime matter** <note>original: "prima materia"; the fundamental, undifferentiated substance of all things.</note> is one and the same; however, they differ among themselves only by accidental action—that is, by more or less boiling, by being tempered or untempered, and by being burning or non-burning. In this, all **Philosophers** <term>Alchemists</term> are in agreement.

For each of these—namely, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> and **sulphur**—is first converted into an earthy substance. Then, from both of these earthy substances, a certain most thin, subtle, and pure smoke is released. Because of the heat in the bowels of the earth, this smoke is boiled and digested, converted into the nature of a certain earth, and thus it takes on a certain fixation and is converted into a metal.

**Note**, the final limit of nature's recommendation and the transmutation of the cooked and the raw—namely, that toward which the artist naturally strives—is the substance of **non-burning sulphur**. When this has been converted, it is the proximate matter of our **real elixir** <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> and of pure metal. It is the primary and closest nature, yet altered by the heat of its own body; specifically, with that alteration through which it can more properly and closely take on its own species and form, in accordance with the will of the **mineral nature** <note>original: "natura mineralis"; the inherent laws governing how minerals "grow" in the earth.</note>. And this...
