The humidity was nothing other than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, raised up from the liquefied body both internally and externally. The qualities of <term>sulphur</term> are mixed with this <term>quicksilver</term> through <term>digestion</term> <note>In alchemy, digestion refers to the process of exposing a substance to a gentle, consistent heat to mature or refine it, mimicking the biological process.</note>. And thus it is altered just as nature requires through its own internal heat; by the conversion of its own nature, it is changed and congealed into <term>sulphur</term>. You can perceive through the laws of nature that no other moisture is more properly and readily converted into the substance of <term>sulphur</term> than that into which the qualities of its own sulphur have been sufficiently introduced through natural ingenuity—which is done through artifice. This moisture is <term>quicksilver</term> in the form of clear water, just like milk in the breasts; and <term>sulphur</term> is like the seed in the testicles. 

That <term>quicksilver</term> does not have any contrariety <note>The presence of opposing qualities (like extreme hot vs extreme cold) that would cause the substance to break apart.</note> arising from its own temperament; therefore, it is necessary that such <term>quicksilver</term> be exceedingly tempered in respect to the temperament of its body. 

Therefore, I notify you that the **matter** of this work is not common <term>quicksilver</term> in its entire substance, etc. <note>The author clarifies that the "Mercury of the Philosophers" is a refined, essential version of the metal, not the ordinary liquid mercury found in shops.</note> The reason why it is necessary to reduce **metal** to the nature of a vapor is because we see all things generated by means of **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio vivo"</note>, from which the metal itself was originally born. For example: a human is born from a father by means of seed, and generates another child by means of seed, and so it is with all others. Therefore, it is the **Mercurial** nature by which we are fed and nourished, for without it there is nothing...

### *Here Follows the Beginning of the Work.*

There are four regimens or stages of this art: The first stage of the regimen is performed by **calcining** <note>original: "calcinando"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note>, that is, the body must first be calcined. The second is by **dissolving** <note>original: "soluendo"</note>, because it must be dissolved. The third is by **distilling** <note>original: "distillando"</note>, because it must be distilled or sublimated. The fourth is by **congealing** <note>original: "congelando"</note> with a gentle fire. And in these four regimens and stages consists the right and true preparation. Therefore the body and the spirit of <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury often represents the volatile, fluid, or "feminine" principle of matter.</note> are necessary to perform the miracles of this thing, as <term>Geber</term> <note>An influential Arab alchemist, historically identified with Jabir ibn Hayyan, known for his systematic approach to chemistry.</note> says. And for this art only two things are required, as <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of the "Hermetic" alchemical tradition.</note> says. Trust consists in two things, to which a third is joined. And he says, "I have seen three faces"—that is, three species—"in one father"—that is, the lineage. Because <term>Morienus</term> <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemical secrets to the King of Egypt.</note> says that three species are sufficient for the whole <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, namely: **white smoke** (which is the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "vis quinta"; the "quintessence" or purest, most refined state of a substance.</note>, namely the heavenly water), the **green lion** <note>A common alchemical symbol often representing acidic vitriol or a specific raw state of metallic matter.</note>, and the **bronze of Hermes** <note>original: "æs Hermetis"; a symbolic term for a specific metallic state or alloy.</note>. From these and with these they prepare the work itself in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.

...the essence of the **sulfur of Mercury** <term>sulphur Mercurii</term> is like the first seed and, at the same time, the mother. Hence it is said: **its father is the Sun** <note>A famous quote from the *Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus*.</note>, that is, sulfur, and **the Moon is its mother**, that is, the proper substance of Mercury. This substance is a subtle watery part mixed with a subtle earthy part and acts as a **solvent** <term>menstruum</term> <note>In alchemy, a *menstruum* is not a biological term but a "solvent" or medium that dissolves and nourishes the matter.</note>. **Its nurse is the earth**, namely the subtle earthy part in which it holds its **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale</term> <note>The essential life-fluid believed by medieval scientists to sustain the existence of all things.</note>.

And the earth is called the mother of the elements because she carries the son in her womb; this is to say that it is necessary to nourish him from the pure **first substance**. This "son" is called the body or the **foliated earth** <term>terra foliata</term>—that is, the spirit and the **dead body** <term>corpus mortuum</term> <note>The physical matter remaining after the "spirit" or "soul" has been extracted during a chemical process.</note>. The work consists of this: that the spirit, in which all power resides, is joined inseparably to its subtle earthy part by a great and sweet skill. 

Join the moist to the dry, and it will rejoice; for the moist is the spirit and the soul, while the dry is called the earth or the dead body. Therefore, the souls of bodies cannot enter in except by means of the spirit. 

And our work is to **make manifest that which is hidden**—namely, the hot and dry qualities—and to **hide that which is manifest**—namely, the cold and moist qualities <note>This refers to the alchemical axiom of "inverting" the elements to reach a state of perfection.</note>. 

Likewise, the **stone** <term>lapis</term> is a moist, watery spirit; but **our Mercury** <note>Alchemists distinguished between "common" mercury (quicksilver) and "philosophical" mercury (the life-force of metals).</note>, which is the **tincture**, is extracted from an incorruptible grain brought forth by divine power. Truly, this Mercury is not the common kind, for common mercury would not coagulate so quickly. Likewise, before all else, it will be beneficial to cleanse the spirit—that is, the Mercury—of its impurities [superfluities], and to draw out from it a substance in which there is nothing superfluous...

**To dye** <term>Tingere</term> is to transform that which is dyed into its own nature through the act of dyeing, and to remain joined with it without any separation, as seen in the nature of the fixer, the dyer, and the dyed.

The **Stone** <term>Lapis</term> is a body composed of the **fifth essence of metals** <term>quinta metallorum essentia</term> <note>The "quintessence" or highest, purest state of matter extracted from the four elements.</note>. This is elsewhere called **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Commonly known as Mercury.</note>, brought out from its potential state into actualization through the mastery of all the principles of this art.

**Oil** <term>Oleum</term> is the unctuous sliminess <note>original: "limositas"; refers to a viscous, oily state of matter.</note> of all metals floating upon the **menstruum** <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent used in alchemy to dissolve and prepare substances.</note> after they have been dissolved. It is essential that bodies be converted into oil, because if they are not converted, they will remain solid within themselves; thus, that which we seek will not be achieved, and the loss of all the principles of this art would follow.

The **menstruum** is that by which the bodies of metals are dissolved through natural dissolution, and their spirits are led from potential into action. According to this definition, it is demonstrated that the dissolution of metals must not be performed except with the aforementioned principle; if it were done otherwise, the result would be nothing in effect.

Moreover, the **Elixir of the philosophers** <term>Elixir philosophorum</term> is composed of three things: namely, the lunar, solar, and mercurial stone.

In the lunar [stone] there exists **white sulfur** <term>sulphur album</term>; in the solar, **red sulfur** <term>sulphur rubeum</term>; and the stone of Mercury embraces both the white and red nature, and—

Neither is it changed from this, nor does it depart from its root and its division from thing into thing without the entry of another thing upon it: except for the **menstrual blood** <note>In medieval science, it was believed that the embryo was formed by the action of the male seed upon the female menstrual blood.</note> from which the semen was [sustained], that is, from blood similar to it, and in it makes its growth. 

And likewise an **egg**, without the entry of another thing upon it, is converted from state to state, and is divided from thing into thing, and finally becomes a flying chick just like the other from which it had its root and principle. And likewise all things born of the earth decay and are changed, and **corruption** <note>Decay or "putrefaction" was considered a necessary stage in alchemy to release the "seed" for new growth.</note> enters upon them; then they sprout and are increased just like the increments from which they had their root and principle.

And because of this, **minerals** <term>mineralia</term> are not nourished so that they depart from their root, but each one returns to that which it was, nor is it converted from this into something else. And whoever says otherwise speaks falsely. This, therefore, is the conversion and division which the wise [philosophers] intend.

It is necessary, therefore, that the perfect body be **subtilized** <note>Refined, made fluid, or reduced to its spiritual essence.</note> before it can possess such power.

->He who dies with me, rises with me.<-

Understand it thus: For the **spirit** <note>In alchemy, the "spirit" usually refers to the volatile parts of a substance that can be evaporated or distilled.</note>, that is, **Mercury**, is the dwelling place of the **soul**—that is, of the Mercurial body—and that spirit is the **philosophers' dry water** <term>aqua sicca philosophorum</term> <note>A paradoxical term used to describe a substance that flows like water but does not wet the hands; it often refers to a highly purified or "philosophical" mercury.</note>. This is specifically the "middle substance" of living Mercury, and it is this spirit that extracts this soul from the perfected bodies. The soul itself is the **tincture** <note>The "tincture" is the concentrated essence or power of transformation that can change the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver.</note> dissolved in the spirit, which is the water of the philosophers.

For just as a common dye is carried in its own water to color cloth, and the colored water runs into the fabric, and then the water departs through drying while the dye remains in the cloth—so too do the wise bring the water in which their tincture resides over their **white, blessed, thirsty earth** <note>The "thirsty earth" refers to a dry, chemically prepared base material (often a metallic oxide or "calx") that is ready to absorb the liquid essence.</note>. The water of the philosophers runs into their earth and is physically extended within it, staining the earth. Then the spiritual water retreats, and the soul remains in the body; this soul is the tincture. It is a subtle, invisible smoke, and its effect does not appear except within a body.

For our entire **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium"; the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is accomplished with our water. All necessary things are made from it and by it. For it dissolves the bodies themselves with a true philosophical dissolution, so that they are converted into the water from which they originated, as **Socrates** <note>Medieval alchemists often attributed their texts to ancient Greek philosophers like Socrates to lend them authority, though these attributions are usually apocryphal.</note> says. The secret of every thing is its life, namely water, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and author of the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> says. The **water of the air** <term>aqua aeris</term> existing between heaven and earth is the life of each and every thing; for this water dissolves the body...

It cites Socrates and Hermes to emphasize that all things originate from and are dissolved by this "philosophical water."</summary>

<meta>This page (524) provides the theoretical foundation for the discussion on page 525. While page 525 describes the metaphorical "dyeing" of the metallic "fabric," this page defines the two types of Mercurial spirits—the preparing and the tinting—that make such a transformation possible.</meta>

# THE BLASTS

<page-num>524</page-num>

...into spirit, and from the dead it creates the living, and it makes a marriage between the man and the woman <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the union of opposites, such as Sulfur and Mercury or the fixed and the volatile.</note>. Indeed, it performs every benefit of the art.

And note that **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver"; the common name for mercury, which was viewed as a "spirit" because of its fluidity and volatility.</note>, or the spirit, is twofold: namely, the **preparing** and the **tinting**.

The **preparing spirit** dissolves the body and purifies it from corrupting causes; it extracts the second spirit existing in the body, which is the **tinting spirit**. It leads the bodies back to itself through dissolution, softens their hardness, and illuminates the bodies. By separating and removing their darkness and impurity from the purest parts, it raises them up and exalts the bodies by leading them back into a sublime nature. It inspires <note>original: *inspirat*; in this context, it refers to the infusion of a spiritual or gaseous quality.</note> and refines the substance while it makes the solid spiritual. These are the benefits and effects of the spirit, or the preparing quicksilver, which prepares the body by extracting from it the tinting spirit. 

Now this spirit—that is, quicksilver—is at first coarse, impure, and **fleeing** <note>original: *fugitivus*; refers to mercury’s tendency to evaporate or "escape" when heated.</note> because of the **sulfur** which it encounters and is mixed with in the passages of the earth. But by the operation of the art, which is performed through **distillation** <note>A process of separating components by heating and cooling.</note> and **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid, used here to purify mercury.</note>, it is renewed, cleaned, purified, cooked down, thickened, and coagulated by means of white and red sulfur.

And this preparing spirit is twofold. The first is a dry, non-viscous vapor of much **acidity** <note>original: *acedinis*; refers to a sharp, penetrating chemical quality rather than just pH.</note>, exceedingly subtle, fleeing the face of the fire easily, having a great power of penetrating, and dissolving the mineral bodies. <page-num>525</page-num>

Using words equivocally, it is called Mercury, but Mercury is a spirit; therefore, by the final definition of reason, it is called a **dry spirit**. It is necessary for such a spirit to be shut away in a well-sealed **flask** <term>ampulla</term> <note>A glass vessel used in alchemical distillation and storage.</note>, and this is according to the intention of **Albertus** <note>Likely referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop whose writings were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note>. For this spirit is generated from **astringent things** <term>rebus ponticis</term> <note>original: *rebus ponticis*; historically referring to bitter, sour, or sharp substances like vitriol or alum, named for the Pontus region.</note>; and he himself calls it a **fiery dry moisture**.

The other **preparing spirit** is moist in its vapor, not oily <term>unctuosus</term>, but viscous <term>viscosus</term> <note>The distinction between "oily" (associated with metals) and "viscous" (associated with the Stone) is a key technical point in this theory.</note>, of the greatest acidity, moderately refined, easily fleeing the harshness of fire and vanishing within it, possessing the power of dissolving bodies and spirits, being water existing within itself. Albertus also holds this view, as do many others, though they speak under the guise of other things. And such a spirit is also called Mercury by an equivocal name, and this is by way of comparison and metaphorical speech. 

For Mercury, as the philosophers say, has the greatest power of altering and penetrating bodies; it does not rest on a flat surface, and it does not wait for the test of fire. Such is the nature of these two spirits, and for that reason both are called Mercury. From these points, receive the true understanding of the sayings of the Philosophers, and your comprehension will be easy here and elsewhere; you will see that the philosophers do not contradict one another, as many have thought. Thus, it must be noted that **oily** is one thing, and **viscous** is another: for the **Stone** <term>lapis</term> is generated from viscous moisture, but **metals** <term>metalla</term> are generated from oily moisture.

The philosophers add: until it is completed as has been said. Sometimes, however, it is fixed in a greater or lesser time, according to the diligence of the operator, and because of the greater or lesser quantity of the pigments <term>pigmentalium; the raw chemical materials or coloring agents used in the work</term>.

Then wash away the salt with fresh water, and dry the mixture by the fire. From here, add to it one part of **white sulfur**, grinding the whole together until it returns to being a single body. However, they do not say this by way of denial <note>original: "per abnegationem"; meaning they are not excluding other methods, but rather highlighting an efficient one</note>. **Arnold** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says: When you wish to ferment the aforementioned medicine, then dissolve it in the stated distilled moisture, as was said above, until it becomes watery like **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>. Then place it in a vessel over the fire in the full **regimen** <term>regimine; the systematic process of controlled heating</term> until the colors appear, as in the first regimen, until you have the **Elixir** as before, both fusible <note>easy to melt</note> and staining <note>tingentem; the ability to "color" or transform base metal into silver or gold</note>. And then the effect of that same elixir is doubled in fermentation, quantity, and **projection** <term>proiectio; the final act of throwing the alchemical catalyst onto the molten base metal to transform it</term>, etc. Since in every dissolution and fixation it acquires for itself ten times the power in multiplication, therefore the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, stained, and melted, the better and more powerfully it works.

Likewise, note concerning the ferment: From the perfect, nothing is made, because it is already perfected, insofar as this matter or art completes it. We have an example: leavened and baked bread is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its final end, nor can you ferment it any further. So it is in gold: pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fi[xed] <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "fi-" likely for "firmum" or "fixum"</note>...

...fixed <note>The word completes "fixum" from the previous page, referring to a substance that can withstand fire without evaporating</note>, and among the philosophers it is impossible to ferment it further unless the **first matter of metals** <term>prima materia metallorum; the primal, formless substance from which all metals originate</term> is obtained, in which it may be dissolved into its first matter and into its mixable elements.

Therefore, let us take that matter from which gold will arise, and by means of the craft, let it be led into the **true ferment of the philosophers** <note>original: "fermentum philosophorum"; the agent that transforms base matter into gold</note>. Let us change this with ingenuity into the perfect matter, or into the form of perfect bodies, and only then let us finally begin the operation. For this reason, many modern workers, even those working according to philosophical principles, are deceived, because they abandon the work at the very point where it ought to be started.

**Note**, water is the **spirit** <term>spiritus; the volatile or gaseous principle</term> that purifies, refines, and whitens the body. And the **ferment** is the **soul** <term>anima; the mediating principle that connects spirit and body</term>, which grants life to the **imperfect body** <note>original: "corpori imperfecto"; usually referring to base metals like lead or copper</note> by means of the water—life which it did not have before—and brings it back into a better form. Even if only one of these were present in our **Stone** <note>The Philosophers' Stone</note>, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it provide the **tincture** <term>tinctura; the power to "stain" or transform the color and nature of a metal</term>; and even if it did, it would fly away into smoke like **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver; known for its volatility and tendency to evaporate when heated</note>, because there would be no vessel within it to hold the tincture.

And in the hour of the greatest **conjunction** <term>coniunctionis; the mystical union of opposites, such as male and female or spirit and body</term>, miracles appear: for then the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul of the imperfect body, and the spirit is joined with the body by means of the soul, and is bound together with it into the color of the ferment; it is joined...

It contains no **contrariety** <note>the conflict between opposing qualities, like hot and cold, which alchemists believed led to decay</note> within itself, and therefore contains no cause of corruption. **Thomas** <note>likely referring to the *Compendium Alchimiae* attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas, though modern scholars consider such works "Pseudo-Aquinas"</note> states this in his compendium, where he distinguishes between an element, an element-composed thing, and the quintessence.

Likewise, **Barfen** <note>A legendary figure and speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the most influential early Latin alchemical texts.</note> says: I command them to whiten the **copper** <term>æs; in alchemy, this usually refers not to common copper, but to the "philosophical" base metal being transformed</term> with white water, with which they make the red copper, namely our copper. For this reason, it is necessary that it first becomes white before it becomes red: because there is no transition from one extreme to the other, or from one contrary to its opposite, except through a mediating middle. That is to say, there is no transition from blackness into yellowness or redness, except with whiteness as a medium; because **yellowing** <term>citrinitas; the stage between the white (albedo) and red (rubedo) marks a successful "digestion" of the matter</term> is essentially caused by a very high or great whiteness combined with a small amount of clear red.

Wherefore nature shows that yellowing is a perfect and complete **digestion** <term>digestio; the process of exposing a substance to steady, gentle heat to mature it</term>. Nor, conversely, can there be a transition from yellow back to white, until the compound is turned into black. Nor can gold be made into indivisible silver unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can the better be made from the worse except through the corruption of itself, because the **generation of one is the corruption of the other** <note>A fundamental Aristotelian and alchemical axiom: for a new form to arise, the old form must be destroyed.</note>. And this happens with the addition of the "tinting thing" <note>the Tincture or Elixir</note> which is known to nature, and thus it is perfected. And then the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance (often likened to yeast) added to the alchemical work to "leaven" the mass and fix its qualities</term> is applied.

The spirit dries the body, and is dried by the body—specifically when it has been perfectly purged of its **phlegm** <note>original: "flegmate"; referring to the watery, impure moisture that must be removed for the "spirit" to stabilize</note>.

Note that in every roasting and decoction by which spirits and bodies are separated and associated <note>the text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; catchword: "tur" from "associantur"</note>...

...[you] ought to know that the soul, being separable from its subject, is not easily separated from the fixed part except in dryness; nor is the living easily joined to the dead, except in moisture. ### *The method of fixing.* <note>original: "Modus figendi"; "fixing" in alchemy refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>

Prepare the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance used to "leaven" or transform the base metal, much like yeast in bread</term>—that is, the body before fermentation—so that it is dissolved and **calcined** <term>calcinatum; reduced to a fine powder by high heat</term>. This means the body is dissolved and calcined by means of **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, such that the quicksilver is separated and removed from it, leaving behind a **calx** <term>calx; the powdery residue left after heating a metal</term> or the most pure ash; for if you have not prepared the ferment properly, it will be worth nothing. 

And similarly, prepare the **non-burning sulfur** <term>sulphur non urens; a purified form of sulfur that does not consume or blacken the metal</term> from the calx through **sublimation** <term>sublimatio; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again in the neck of the vessel</term>, so that it becomes simple and "living." For if you do not mix this into the **Elixir** <note>the "Medicine" or "Philosopher's Stone" in liquid or powder form</note>, the body upon which the **projection** <term>proiectio; the final step of throwing the Elixir onto a molten base metal to transmute it</term> of sulfur is made will not be colored. And if you do not cleanse the body that you wish to mix into the Elixir, the body will neither direct the spirit nor retain it. Furthermore, if you do not sublimate this kind of sulfur which you wish to put into the Elixir, the resulting gold and silver will be very dark.

And if you do not cleanse the spirit, it will not withstand the fire, because an impure spirit cannot be joined to the body **in its smallest parts** <note>original: "per minima"; refers to a perfect, microscopic union of substances</note>. You must also be very cautious to make the Elixir a medium between hard and soft; because unless you know how to do this, the gold and silver will not be fit for working—that is, for hammering or for casting. For the medicine ought to be of a more subtle and more liquid substance, since these are bodies of greater fixation and retention than quicksilver is in its own nature, upon which they are projected. For as **Euclid** <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-Euclidean alchemical text common in the Middle Ages, rather than the Greek mathematician</note> says:

Our final secret is to possess the **medicine** <term>medicina; the Philosopher's Stone in its healing or transformative capacity</term> that flows before the **flight of Mercury** <note>original: "ante Mercurij fugam"; meaning the substance must melt and act before the mercury component can evaporate or "flee" from the heat</note>. ### *Regarding the weights of the ferment, sulfur, and Mercury.*

Note, for it must first be understood that the total amount of the **volatile** <term>volatilis; a substance that evaporates easily when heated</term> must not exceed the total amount of its cleansed, **fixed** <term>fixi; a substance that remains solid and stable under high heat</term> body. Otherwise, the bond of the "betrothal" would be turned into the flight of the non-fixed spirit and the volatile sulfur. The volatile must not exceed the sum of the fixed material united with it. Whence **Plato** <note>referring to an alchemical work traditionally but likely falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher</note> says: If a small amount of sulfur is cast upon a great quantity of the body, so that it holds power over it, it converts the body into a powder, the color of which will be like the color of the body upon which the **spirit of gold or silver** is cast. ## *Note on the ferment.*

It must be noted that when the Elixir is joined with **bodies** <note>referring to the base metals to be transformed</note>, it is necessary that it be joined *per minima* <term>per minima; a Latin phrase meaning "by the smallest parts," similar to mixing at a molecular level</term>, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and saint often cited as an authority in alchemy</note> says. A powerful and useful combination can never be made with solid things unless they are first **dissolved into waters** <note>turned into a liquid or "philosophical" solution</note>, and then mixed with one another; and then, in warm places with natural heat (or a heat proportional to it) acting upon them, they connect themselves through vapor over a suitable period of time. For it is necessary first to dissolve the Elixir, and afterwards to prepare and dissolve the **body** just like the Elixir, and then finally to take and join the solutions: namely, **three parts** of the Elixir and **one part** of the aforementioned bodies. Afterwards, it is necessary to congeal this whole and dissolve it again, and congeal it, and thus repeat the process until the whole is made into one without any separation. This entire process is completed through the benefit of our **Mercurial water**: for with this, the Elixir is dissolved and prepared, and with this, the bodies are dissolved and prepared. For this water is the agent of cleansing, joining, dissolving, whitening, and making red.

### *On the multiplication or augmentation of the stone.*

First, note what **augmentation** <term>augmentum; the process of increasing the power or quantity of the alchemical medicine</term> is. From which we see that augmentation is the addition to a pre-existing quantity. And augmentation in quality and goodness is to **dissolve** <term>solvere; to turn a solid into a liquid state</term> and **coagulate** <term>coagulare; to turn a liquid back into a solid</term> the **tincture** <term>tinctura; the active medicinal essence capable of transforming metals</term> itself; that is, to **imbibe** <term>imbibere; to soak a solid in a liquid until it is absorbed</term> it with our Mercury and to dry it out.

Or do it this way: Take one part of the prepared tincture and dissolve it in three parts of our **Mercury** <term>Mercurius; in this context, the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a specialized solvent, not common quicksilver</term>; then place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes throughout the process, as expressed above, until it is dried and becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and imbibe it again, and dry it as above; and the more times you do this, the more parts you will gain, and it **tints** <note>original: "tingit"; the ability of the Stone to spread its color and quality through a base metal</note> even further, as Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says.

Augmentation in quantity is this: Take three parts of the **fixed matter** <note>The stable, solid substance that has already undergone fixation.</note> that tints—that is, of the prepared tincture—and one part of the Mercury of the Philosophers, and place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes, as above, and dry it so that it becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and imbibe it again, and dry it, etc., as above. And the water—that is, the **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver" or mercury</term> or Mercury—adds or gives no more weight to the body except for as much of the metallic moisture as remains.

<page-num>570</page-num>

<header>->TRUMPET<-</header>

These are the words of Calidius, son of Isydorus <note>original: "Calidius filius Isydori"; likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and legendary figure in alchemy.</note>. Likewise, **multiplication** <term>multiplicatio; the process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical Stone</term> in quantity is achieved by mixing the **medicine** <term>medicina; the "Stone" in its active state</term> in a crucible with common quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo vulgi"; ordinary mercury as opposed to the "philosophical" mercury used in earlier stages.</note>. This quicksilver, by the admixture of the Stone, is converted into a red or black powder. And repeatedly, let some of that powder of quicksilver be placed upon more quicksilver, and it is converted again into powder; and thus you shall perform repetitions of the powder of quicksilver upon other quicksilver, until the quicksilver is no longer converted into powder, but remains converted into **perfect metal** <note>original: "metallum perfectum"; referring to gold or silver.</note>. And this happens because the strength of the medicine is tempered by the addition of the quicksilver.

Likewise, the multiplication of the **tincture** <term>tinctura; the concentrated essence capable of coloring and transforming metals</term> is nothing other than the increase and multiplication of natural heat, which is **non-burning sulfur** <term>sulphur non vrens; a stable, essential "fire" or spiritual seed within the matter that matures it without destroying it</term> within the matter of quicksilver. ### *The philosopher's stone is multiplied in three ways.*

The first way is done by the repetition of the known **corruption** <note>original: "corruptio"; in alchemy, this refers to the necessary decay or breaking down of a substance before it can be reborn in a higher form</note> back to the beginning; that is, by corrupting the stone through dissolution and **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio; a stage of blackness and decomposition seen as essential for spiritual and physical purification</term>, and through the joining of the elements, and burial in air or in earth, and through the **decoctions** <term>decoctio; a process of boiling or heating to extract or concentrate properties</term> of air and common fire.

And this applies to other particular works, through the joining of the elements with the **foliated earth** <note>original: "terra foliata"; a purified, white, flaky state of the matter often compared to "leaves" or salts</note>, and decoction by common fire, in a burial in **dung** <note>original: "fimi"; horse dung was frequently used in laboratories as a source of steady, gentle, moist heat for "incubating" the alchemical vessel</note>.

Likewise, both types of multiplication happen at once if you lead the medicine, already multiplied in quantity, to the two aforementioned **wheels** <term>rotas; refers to the cyclical, repetitive stages of the alchemical process, often visualized as a rotating wheel of transformation</term>, and do as has been said.

### *The method for projecting all the things prescribed above can be tested in this way.*

Let one part of the **medicine** <term>medicina; the finished Philosopher's Stone or Elixir</term> be taken, and ten parts of crude, purified **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij crudi purgati"; quicksilver</note>, in such a way that the Mercury is heated by the fire until it begins to fume. From that moment, let the medicine be projected <note>projectio; the act of "throwing" the Elixir onto the molten metal to initiate transformation</note> upon it; it will immediately flow, penetrating into the smallest parts. Then, with the fire kept vigorous, let the molten Mercury be collected. Take a small portion of this, and place it upon the fire with an equal amount of its own **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij viui"; liquid quicksilver</note>, and let the weight be tested. If the added Mercury has notably receded <note>meaning it evaporated or "fled" from the heat because it was not fixed or transformed</note>, then the medicine is not sufficient for further parts. If, however, the body has not been notably diminished within the body, but the matter is still brittle, or too soft or hard, then let a small portion of this be taken again, along with an equal amount of crude Mercury, and let the process proceed through all steps as has been said, until the intent is achieved.

...the [transmu]tation is manifest enough. For everything that is silver, it makes into gold in color, substance, permanence, weight, ductility, melting point, hardness, and softness. Regarding the third <note>likely the third "virtue" or power of the philosopher's stone</note>, it is written that it transforms stones into precious gems, as was mentioned above. In the book *Sextariae* <note>original: *Sextariae*; likely referring to the *Liber de Sexaginta* or "Book of Sixty," a medieval alchemical compilation</note>, it is said that jaspers, hyacinths <note>a blue or reddish-brown zircon or gemstone</note>, red and white corals, emeralds, chrysolites, and sapphires can be formed from this very matter. # THE CORRECTION OF FOOLS, A SHORT TREATISE
<note>original: CORRECTIO FATVORVM, TRACTATVLVS; this title suggests a work intended to correct the errors of "sophists" or "fools" who misunderstand the true principles of alchemy.</note>

## Prologue to the same.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' inside a square border, featuring ornate leaf and vine motifs.</image-desc>

*SINCE* the correction <note>original: emendatio; can also mean improvement or restoration to a better state</note> of all things is the increase of the thing itself: Therefore, it is written in many sayings of the **Philosophers** <term>original: Philosophonū [Philosophorum]; likely referring to Aristotle or the collective wisdom of ancient sages</term> that nature is improved through **art** <term>original: ars; in this context, "art" refers specifically to the alchemical craft or human intervention</term> beyond the movement it possessed in its first form. For no art can labor except by the mediation of nature, since nature itself labors intrinsically and secretly within the art through the administration of the craftsman. From this it follows that the imitation of nature's power is both an increase and a labor, and an augmentation of the thing itself: because nature completes its own degree, as much as it is naturally able to complete, and it cannot surpass that unless it is hindered by some contrary force. However, art does not truly transcend nature by creating a new nature through simple labor. And for this reason it is said that art imitates nature, not that it builds a new one, but that it refines the power of that nature. Because of this, art begins to perfect where nature leaves off—namely, to uncover the subtle nature enclosed within a thing, and to make it manifest. For this reason, the mineral ore generates metals, yet it cannot generate **tinctures** <term>original: tincturas; the transformative substances or "colors" capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term>, although it truly contains a full tincture hidden within itself, just as the Philosopher says:

Nature contains within itself those things which it requires, and those by which it is perfected, unless it should be moved by art and operation. ### ON THE UTILITY OF STUDY.

**Study** removes ignorance and leads the human **intellect** back to true **knowledge** and to the **science** of any thing. Therefore, it is necessary above all to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work <note>original: suauis operis; likely referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy, often described in sensory or emotional terms by practitioners</note>, and to sharpen one's wit through **physical** <term>original: physica; here referring to natural philosophy or the laws of the physical world</term> sayings, since the knowledge of **truth** is found within them. If those who labor do not despise study, they will sweetly taste the fruit that comes from it.

However, those who shrink from study yet still wish to labor should consider whether their art is truly an imitation of **nature**, which art is meant to refine. For it is impossible for such a person to prepare the secrets of the philosophers to a perfect end. Regarding these people, the wise say that they approach practice like a **donkey to a dinner**, not knowing what they stretch their snouts toward, except insofar as the external senses—without intellect—lead them to the fodder through sight and taste.

Thus these "donkeys," lacking good and true principles, fruitful study, and the knowledge of natures, seek to perfect the works of nature and the secret of all **philosophy**. They seek that best work which adorns a man with character, enriches him with benefits, aids the poor, and keeps the **human body** safe, providing **health**, as can be said regarding the power of that nature. ### First Chapter.

## *How many parts of minerals there are.*
### Chapter II.

Mineral bodies are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, the metallic part and the mineral part. The metallic part refers to the metals which derive their origin from **Mercury** <note>original: Mercurio; in alchemical thought, Mercury is the "mother" or the fluid, feminine principle that combines with Sulfur to form all metals</note>. The mineral part refers to those things that do not draw their origin from Mercury. Examples of metals include gold, Silver <note>original: Luna</note>, Mercury, Tin <note>original: Iupiter</note>, Iron <note>original: Mars</note>, Lead <note>original: Saturnus</note>, and electrum <note>a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note>. Examples of minerals include salts, inks <note>original: atramenta; refers to various metallic sulfates used for making dyes and writing fluids</note>, alum, vitriol, arsenic, and orpiment <note>original: auripigmentum; a gold-colored arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. These are distinct from the metals that derive their origin from Mercury.

Moreover, all metals that have taken their origin from Mercury are **ductile** <term>original: ductibilia; the property of a metal that allows it to be hammered thin or shaped without breaking</term> and **meltable**. This is because their material is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in such a strong combination that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that watery substance is solidified by cold even more so after the action of heat, and they will therefore be ductile or workable by a smith. Water alone does not solidify except when combined with an earthy dryness that alters its wateriness, since there is no oily moisture within them. Because their solidification is caused by this earthy dryness, they are not easily dissolved or melted except by the action of intense heat upon them, according to how strongly and firmly they have been bound together.

### Chapter III.

The nature and substance of all meltable things come from quicksilver <note>original: argento vivo; another name for Mercury</note>, because [the metal] is solidified by means of that same quicksilver from the vapor or heat of white or red non-burning sulfur. This is because every dry thing naturally drinks its own moisture so that it may be unified in its parts.

Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that solidifies the quicksilver is composed of an earthy, subtle, and airy substance, **boiled** and **digested** <term>original: decocta & digesta; alchemical terms for the maturation of substances through steady heat, mimicking the Earth's natural processes</term> from the first mixture, united to itself by the action of heat, and afterwards raised, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of solidifying quicksilver into metallic bodies. But when sulfur is simple or burning, it causes perfection or imperfection in metals, as the following example will show: that their first material becomes quicksilver, because when they are melted, they are converted into it by heat. It is certain that they were previously quick[silver]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "argentum [vivum]" and continues on the next page.</note>

## *On the generation of Mercury and which metals are generated from it.*

### Chapter IV.

Quicksilver <term>original: Argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term> in its first root is composed of a white, subtle earth, highly sulfurous, strongly mixed with clear water until it becomes a single substance. This substance does not rest on a flat surface, nor does it stick to what touches it, because of the dryness that has altered the watery nature within it. It is, however, homogeneous in its nature: for either the whole remains in the fire and is fixed, or the whole flies away in smoke, since it is non-combustible and airy. And this is a sign of perfection. Therefore, when it first flows heated through sulfurous earth, it ascends to the top. Hence its nature is such that it is refined <note>original: subtilietur; made subtle or thin</note> by heat.

Nevertheless, by continual sublimation <term>original: sublimatione; the process of vaporizing a substance and then allowing it to condense back into a solid, used here to describe nature's way of purifying minerals</term> it is greatly purified, boiled down, and thickened, and is gradually congealed by means of white and red sulfur.

Since sulfur is dissolved many times, the sublimated quicksilver is first coagulated and made waxy <note>original: inceratum; an alchemical state where a substance becomes soft and pliable like wax, a stage preceding the final hardening into metal</note> by the action of heat, until over the course of thousands of years, by the successive work of nature, it is coagulated into a perfect metal. Indeed, from this substance, nature itself works metals within "mineral vessels" <note>referring to the natural cavities and veins in the Earth's crust where ores form</note>. In these works, therefore, it is necessary to imitate nature, for whoever...

If, however, the sulfur is bad and weak, but the Mercury is of good substance, it converts it into **copper** <term>original: æs; often used for bronze or copper alloys</term>. 

If the quicksilver is heavy, earthy, and unclean, and the sulfur is likewise unclean, foul-smelling, earthy, and of a "fixed" <note>in alchemy, "fixed" substances resist the action of fire and do not evaporate</note> substance, then **iron** <term>original: ferrum</term> is made from it, which thereafter is not easily melted. 

**Tin** <term>original: stagnum</term>, on the other hand, is seen to have good quicksilver, but bad sulfur that is not well mixed; for this reason, it causes a "grating" <note>original: stridorem; tin is famous for the "cry of tin," a crackling sound made when the metal is bent or bitten, which alchemists attributed to its poor internal mixture</note> between the teeth. 

**Lead** <term>original: plumbum</term> possesses a coarse, bad quicksilver that is of an ill and foul flavor and weak power; thus, it is continually corrupted by the violence of fire. 

In this way, the metallic bodies differ from quicksilver according to whether there is "foreign" or "burning" sulfur present within them. This is considered so because of the power residing in them: a large quantity of sulfur is an imperfection, while a large quantity of quicksilver is a perfection. This is because quicksilver is non-combustible and airy, whereas sulfur burns and is burned, and in every work, it hinders perfection. 

These are the words of **Aristotle** in the fourth <note>Original: "Aristotelis quarto"; referring to Book IV of Aristotle's *Meteorology*, which was the primary authority for the belief that metals were formed from "exhalations" (vapor and smoke) in the earth</note>...

But metallic bodies cannot be made from them artificially, since they are of another nature; they did not take their origin with the metals from the proximate first matter—namely with Mercury—but from quicksilver <note>original: ex argento vivo; the author appears to be making a distinction here between "Mercury" as a philosophical principle and "quicksilver" as a common substance</note>. I do not deny that metals can be purified or dissolved with these minerals, or that a "sophistical" <note>meaning deceptive or counterfeit</note> form can be introduced through them to deceive men, by which the blackness of lead can be wiped away; nevertheless, lead always remains lead. 

Thus, craftsmen can perform "congealings" <note>coagulations or solidifications</note> through them—that is, they can extract the moisture from Mercury using dry substances, so that the Mercury appears to be coagulated. ## Chapter VI.

Since it has been stated that the sulfur which causes metals to form is the element of metals along with Mercury, I now set forth the difference in the generation of Mercury and of sulfur, although they both certainly cause the metal to be—namely, through essential Mercury and through sulfur on the accidental side <note>In alchemy, "essential" refers to the core nature, while "accidental" refers to external qualities like color or hardness</note>. ### *Question.*

Since the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, the standard authority in medieval science</note> generally speaks to the effect that sulfur coagulates, it must be said that it does not. In what way, then, can it inspire life in others? Therefore, consider by these things that common sulfur is not the sulfur of the philosophers, since the sulfur of the philosophers <term>sulphur philosophorum; the refined, spiritual principle of sulfur</term> is a simple living fire, bringing life to other dead bodies and ripening them, so that it supplies the defect of nature; for it is of an overflowing ripeness, according as it is perfect in its own nature and is more and more purified through the art. Whence Avicenna says: "Such sulfur is not found upon the earth, except insofar as it emerges in those bodies of the Sun and the Moon <note>alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>, and in another thing, which is that which is told to no one unless it be revealed to them by God." In the Sun, however, it is more perfect: because it is more digested and cooked <term>decoctum; ripened or refined by heat</term>.

This happens because of the greater digestion performed by the natural heat existing within me. In this same way, you must follow nature through art: likewise boil, digest, and mature the matter substantially, since nature already actually contains within itself the natural fire by which it is ripened. Other things do not possess this quality, and therefore they cannot bestow it. 

In the moon <note>Luna, the alchemical symbol for silver</note> there is nothing but simple white sulfur; however, it is not yet digested like the red, nor has it been stripped of its blackness by the action of the heat which it naturally contains within itself. Rather, the form of fire is covered and hidden, acting within it more through art than through nature. And for this reason, it is not impossible that art, with nature mediating, may digest and perfect this further, since it naturally intends to be perfected; but on its own it cannot, unless it is moved by art and manual operation. But these labors, as I believe, do not come to a man of a "stiff neck" <note>A biblical idiom for a person who is stubborn, proud, or unwilling to learn</note>. And therefore true gold is not made, unless it be made...

### *How gold cures the infirmities of men and the sick bodies of metals. Chapter XI.*

Since, moreover, among both common people and Philosophers <note>alchemists often referred to themselves simply as "Philosophers"</note>, gold holds the form that, remaining in its primary disposition, it may cure leprosy and have many other virtues, this is because of its complete digestion <term>digestio; the process of being "cooked" or perfected by nature's internal heat over time</term>. For the excellence of the fire acting within it consumes all bad humors <note>In ancient medicine, humors were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which caused disease if unbalanced</note> existing in sick bodies, whether caused by a hot or cold cause.

The Philosophers <note>the respected historical authorities of the alchemical tradition</note> knew the truth; they therefore based this science upon the movement of nature. Some, however, write in their faulty and argumentative books: "Beware of its odor, lest it kill you." Behold, what kind of medicine and contradiction is this, which induces death when it ought to heal! It is no wonder that intoxicating things composed of poisons can do such things. See, you fools, how your works differ from the work of nature.

Yet by no means can art so separate the parts joined in generation that they are simply transmuted <term>transmutatio: the change of one substance into another</term> back into the elements they once were. Since primary nature has changed one quality into another, art is well able to separate them in such a way—as the moist from the dry, or the cold from the hot. But nonetheless, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part from the natural mixture; and because of this, they can be joined back together by art just as they were divided. If it were not for the fact that one quality participates in the nature of another—for instance, **water** in the nature of **earth** through coldness, or **air** in the nature of **water** through moisture, and so on for the rest—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed, since the elements would be in their simplest state just as they were before. Moreover, regarding why the philosophers entrusted this science to posterity and the "sons of wisdom" through distant similarities and obscure allegories, **Hamul** <note>Also known as Ibn Umail or "Senior Zadith," a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose work was highly influential in the Latin West.</note> in the book of the *Senior* posits the chief reason: so that they might attribute it to the glorious God, who would reveal it to whom He wished and withhold it from whom He wished. Also, **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> records in his *Book of Lights*: "For if I wished to explain everything according to how it truly is, there would no longer be any place for prudence, since the fool would be made equal to the wise." ...reciting that God is in all things, or rather, all things are in God, just as all numbers are contained within unity, or as all the straight lines of a circle meet at its center. Since unity is the common measure, fountain, and origin of all numbers—containing every number uniquely joined within itself—it is the principle of all multiplicity. In a similar way, created things relate to their creator. And just as the individual human soul exists as the ruler of its body, present to the whole body and to each of its parts, so similarly God is everywhere in this world. He fills it, moderates it, and continually preserves it through the power which He liberally rains down upon created things daily from the perennial fountain of His spirit. 

Hence, we correctly use a certain similarity to the "soul of nature" to describe God—or the power of God by which He sustains all things—calling Him the "intermediate soul" or the **soul of the world** <note>original: "anima mundi." This is a Neoplatonic concept suggesting that the entire universe is a living, breathing entity, though the author clarifies the Christian stance on this below.</note>. This is not because the world itself is a living animal—a notion which can be dismissed partly in Christian Metaphysics and partly in this consideration of the **stone** <term>stone: Referring to the "Philosopher's Stone" (lapis philosophorum). In this alchemical context, the author uses the search for the Stone as a framework for understanding how divine spirit inhabits dense matter.</term>. Although it is persuasive to weave those loftier aspects of nature into a more polished style of speech, I have chosen here to proceed in a more "pedestrian" prose <note>original: "pedestri sermone" — meaning a straightforward, plain style of writing rather than poetic or overly rhetorical language.</note>. 

We place that soul of the world primarily in the **sun**. For there is nothing in the very circle of the firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars or the heavens.</note>, besides the soul itself, which displays a greater likeness of God than light...

### *On Nature. Chapter IX.*

We assert that nature is a certain force implanted in things, procreating like from like. For nature generates, increases, and nourishes all things. Therefore, it holds within itself the names of all things. An animal is from nature; a stone, wood, a tree, and the bodies you see are from nature and its bond. Nature is the ligament of the elements and the power of mixing, which effects the mixtures of elements in any thing of this sublunary <term>sublunary: literally "below the moon," referring to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</term> world, and it has impressed the form suitable to its species: through which that thing is distinguished and separated from any other thing. 

Nor is nature of any one color, yet it is the participant and producer of all colors; it is also of no weight or quality, but finally is the fertile mother of all qualities and things. What then is nature? God is nature, and nature is God. Understand it thus: from God arises something...

### *What the Philosophers sought, and the nature of that which they desired, wherein the ethereal spirit is held to be the chariot of the soul.*

->*Chapter X.*<-

The stone which the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists, often called "natural philosophers" or "philosophers by fire."</note> seek is an **invisible and impalpable spirit**. It is a **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a potent substance or "stain" capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</term> and a staining spirit. This is what another spirit, one both visible and palpable, has hidden away in its innermost depths. In the same way, the Philosophers have left this same spirit to us unexplained, hidden under a veil of riddles. That stone is the **fifth thing** <note>original: "quintum à quatuor segregatum". This refers to the "Quintessence," the purified fifth element that exists beyond the four classical elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note> separated from the four. ### Chapter XI.

Such a bond, however, cannot be easily obtained because of the incredibly strong compaction <note>original: "compactionem". In white, all colors exist, and from it, all others—if I may put it this way—seem to be colored. White and black are themselves colors by nature, and indeed the extremes: from whose manifold mixing and proportion with one another, we believe the intermediate colors, as they are called, arise. We also believe that from a certain mingling of white and black, **redness** <note>original: "rubedinē." This refers to the Rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone reaches its full power.</note> is forged.

We call this whiteness the **white stone**, the **white sun**, the **full moon**, the **calcined moon**, **white silver**, **fruitful white earth** (both purified and calcined), **white lime**, the **salt of metals**, and the **calcined body**; we name it by many other names as well. Furthermore, it is called **living earth** and **living white sulfur** when the soul has been introduced into the body and every hindrance has been removed.

Here we solve this question: whether the "earth" should be of the nature of air or of fire. We say it is both at once. For if it were only fiery, it would be burned into the ashes of the dead. But if it were only of the nature of air, it would become volatile and vanish while attempting to "dye" <note>original: "tingendis." In alchemy, "tinging" or dyeing refers to the process of transmutation, where the Stone "colors" or changes the nature of a base metal into a noble one.</note> the metals.

But what shall I mention concerning the fire by which the dissolution of the earth is achieved? Behold the heat in the bowels of the earth, which nature alone provides. There you may seem to perceive almost nothing, yet it is instigated by the heat of the sun and ascends within the metal-bearing mountains...

To which the spirit replies:

> I shall certainly do so, but wretched me, I am forced to depart, when [I see] you [valued] above all **precious stones**...

...to be sought. After our stone has been made white, we say that our son has been born. Even though the boy is now a perfect human, consisting of body and soul, he is not yet able to generate other offspring until he is first nourished by the food of his own nature, until he reaches an age mature for generation.

We have received from those ancient philosophers, who worked by nature alone, that their living water <note>original: "aquam suam vivam" — a term for the mercurial solvent used to dissolve metals</note> was divided into two parts. When they had reached a fixed whiteness <term>whiteness: original "albedo," the stage of the Great Work signifying the purification of the matter into "white sulfur" or silver</term> with one part of the water, they turned it red with the other reserved part, or perhaps even by fire alone.

Dissolving that redness <term>redness: original "rubedo," the final stage of the Great Work, signifying the perfection and fixation of the medicine</term> with the other part of the reserved water, they reduced it once more to its "first essence," so to speak. They labored in almost all things just as they had from the beginning, but with a greater diligence of both fire and effort; and they believed this repetition to be a truer or greater augmentation <term>augmentation: the process of increasing the quantity or the transformative power (the "projection") of the finished stone</term>. 

Wherefore the first philosophers used a much longer time in completing the stone. However, those born later and their successors are accustomed to finish it in the course of a year. For this reason, they might wish to tincture the white stone—with which they operate on the moon <note>original: "luna" — the alchemical name for silver</note>—entirely with lunar seed, or by adding other spirits to it, namely white spirits, drawn from Jupiter <note>original: "Iove" — the alchemical name for tin</note> and Saturn <note>original: "Saturno" — the alchemical name for lead</note> through sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again, used to purify "volatile" spirits</term>...

We distinguish the **mineral stone** in three ways:
1. The **Stone of the Philosophers** is made from gold alone and nature alone; it is the more sublime one, which the philosophers claim can cure all illnesses. 
2. Another is the **simple stone**, produced when only the root and **sulfur of gold or silver** is augmented at the end by the spirits of inferior bodies. Here, the weights—one part to three, or two parts to seven—are discussed as set forth in the *Minor Assembly* <note>original: "Minori Turba," likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, requiring only sulfur, either of gold or of silver.

...to you, **son of philosophy** <note>A traditional address to a student or initiate of the alchemical arts</note>, I might explain certain obscure propositions, from which you might most easily be able to resolve other objections put to you. The philosophers say that their **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note> is found everywhere, in mountains and in caverns. From that poorly understood proposition, I am persuaded that all errors have flowed down to posterity—those who have worked with sheep's blood, hair, and other vain and foreign substances. 

Understand it in this way: Just as the **celestial sun itself** <note>original: "solipse cœlestis"</note> is everywhere in this **greater world** <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> through its rays, so this **earthly sun**—that is, gold—is everywhere in the whole **glass vessel**—that is, the **lesser world** <note>the microcosm, represented here by the chemist's flask</note>. In the **mountains**, that is, the "head" or top of the glass vessel and the sky; and in the **caverns**, that is, in the bottom of the glass and the earth. They say the stone is born on two mountains: in the mountain of heaven and the earth; understand this to mean within the glass vessel. 

Furthermore, they assert that their stone is in all things—that is, in all metals, which are their "things." Likewise, the stone is in every thing—that is, **nature** is in every thing. And because nature has all names within itself, and nature is the whole world, therefore the stone has many names and is said to be in every thing, although it may be closer in one thing than in another, since the philosophers demand only the **generative nature** of metals. Whence they say: the **rich** <note>original: "diuites," referring to noble or "perfect" metals</note>—that is, perfect bodies, such as gold and silver—possess that nature just as the **poor** <note>original: "pauperes"</note>—that is, **imperfect metals**—do. Nevertheless, the nature of gold or silver is more perfect and more permanent in fire than in the other metals. Also, the philosophers [call] the fixed thing and...

...they seek an enduring thing which rules the whole world, such as the **sun** or the **moon**. Whence in ancient times they called the sun the **lord of the world** <note>original: "mundi dominum"</note>: in which is the life for healing all things, which creates the day by its motion, as well as the night, and illuminates the entire world with its brilliance. Wherefore the sun says: **I am the stone.** Or: **In me is the stone.** The philosophers also say that the **work of the stone is the work of a woman, and the play of children.** <note>These are two of the most famous alchemical paradoxes. "Work of a woman" suggests that once the process is started, it requires only the patient, gentle heat of a hearth; "play of children" suggests the work is easy for those who know the secret, or refers to the way the chemical elements "toil" and "jump" in the glass.</note>

The **woman** is sometimes the earth, and sometimes <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury is the "feminine" principle of fluidity and transformation</note>, which seems to complete the whole work. The **children play with the stone**, that is, the three elements play with the earth, or the "lower bodies" play with the **golden stone** when they have increased it at the end of the process. Likewise, the children play with the stone and throw it away; this means the ignorant and unskillful throw the "earth" itself to the bottom when they have performed <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind</note>. Some philosophers have compared the work of the stone to the **creation of the world**.

Similarly, they compare it to the **generation of man** and his natural development. But later philosophers have hidden this skill not only in modern words, but also in **painted images**. I myself have seen, depicted with a most beautiful brush, a **naked virgin**, in the flower of her youth, with ivory-white hair, dark eyes, and cheeks of blending white and red, whose breasts were milky and perfectly smooth and rounded. 

And this virgin was so remarkable for the brilliant whiteness of her whole body, and so beautifully adorned and shaped with all the gifts of nature, that she could be considered most worthy of a **royal bedchamber**—a woman for whom all philosophers, both the ancient ones and the moderns, were desperately in love. <note>This "virgin" is an allegory for the pure, white stage of the alchemical process, known as the *Albedo*. Her beauty represents the perfection of the material before it is transformed into the "Red King" or the final Stone.</note>

But just as an unclean cloth—not unlike sulfur—cannot be purified without water, so the nature of sulfur is not washed without water. **To wash is to dissolve; to dissolve is to purify.** The **water** is **Mercury**; it is the key itself. It alone opens the body and whitens the sulfur; once it is whitened, the Mercury recedes along with the impurity. I would say you flourish with singular learning if you are able to remove that [impurity]. It is the impediment and eternal death.

...should be perpetual, even until the final judgment <note>original: "indicium extremum"; this likely refers to the Last Judgment, implying the permanent transmutative effects of the stone</note>. It heals human bodies from every sickness until natural death. **Question**: Of what sort and what thing is the soul of the human body? **Response.** It is a living fire of celestial life; and it possesses within itself the soul, the mediating nature <term>mediating nature: the "Anima Media," a vital alchemical concept of an intermediary force that bridges the spiritual and material worlds</term>. By the soul, the mediating nature, God is called the creator of all things that are in the world. **Question.** Did Virgil <note>In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the poet Virgil was often reimagined as a powerful magician and alchemist</note> possess the stone? **Response.** Not only did he himself possess the stone, but many Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi"; in this context, it refers specifically to alchemists or "lovers of wisdom" who sought the Great Work</note> possessed it, and they wrote about it in many ways under obscure names and through many operations. **Question.** How and why is it called a stone? **Response.** I tell you, "stone" is its name, and the freedom is not given to me to reveal anything further to you. **Question.** In how much time can the stone be brought to its conclusion? **Response.** Twelve months are necessary from the first day of its beginning. In thirty days, earth is generated from Saturn <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for lead</term>, or the nature of the earth causes Saturn to grow. In one hundred days, quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> grows in water. In sixty completed days, air grew from Jupiter <term>Jupiter: the alchemical name for tin</term>. In the other days of the year, fire grows from the Sun <term>the Sun: the alchemical name for gold</term>. At the turning point of the year, the soul, the mediating nature, descends from heaven into this earth, and mortifies <note>original: "mortificat"; in alchemical practice, "mortification" is the process of breaking down a substance, often associated with a symbolic death before its eventual purification</note> the superior and inferior powers. It is an image of manifold victory for the ending of the war in the heart of their belly, even until the perpetual sign of fire. I shall tell you no more.

->T H E   E N D.<-

<summary>This concluding page of the dialogue describes the alchemical "Stone" as a universal medicine and details a twelve-month symbolic timeline for its creation involving the planetary metals Saturn, Jupiter, and the Sun. It reinforces the stone's divine origin and the secrecy maintained by past "Philosophers" like Virgil.</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, Anima Media, Virgil the Magician, Alchemical Timing, Saturn, Jupiter, Sun, Mortification, Universal Medicine</keywords>
